#6516. Puppy Chow Balls

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Puppy chow is our favorite Midwestern snack, and it’s the inspiration these holiday-ready truffles. You’ll find all the same ingredients—peanut butter, Chex, chocolate and confectioners’ sugar—but with a truffle redesign that’s sophisticated enough for a Christmas dessert table (and that keeps hands considerably less messy!).

Like puppy chow, Chex cereal (crushed for easier rolling) and peanut butter are melted together to make the crunchy truffle filling. Each truffle is enrobed in a thick layer of melted chocolate then coated generously with confectioners’ sugar. These puppy chow truffles are a two- to three-bite affair and totally remind me of those big puppy chow clusters everyone fights over.

In a large microwave-safe bowl, heat the peanut butter in 30-second increments until it’s completely melted, stirring occasionally. Add 2 tablespoons of confectioners’ sugar and stir until smooth. Add the crushed Chex and stir until everything is well combined.

Scoop the puppy chow truffles by the tablespoonful onto wax-paper-lined baking sheets. Freeze them until they’re firm, about 30 minutes.

In a microwave-safe bowl, melt the semisweet chocolate and shortening at 50% power, and stir until they’re smooth. Dip each puppy chow ball into the melted chocolate and shake off the excess. Place the puppy chow truffles on a waxed paper–lined baking sheet.

Place the confectioners’ sugar in a large airtight container or resealable bag. In batches, add the puppy chow balls and shake them in the bag until they’re well coated in confectioners’ sugar. Store the puppy chow truffles in an airtight container.

Store puppy chow truffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to four days. They can also last in the fridge for up to one week.

Yes, you can freeze puppy chow truffles, but wait to coat them with confectioners’ sugar until after they’ve thawed. To freeze the puppy chow truffles, place them on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them for one hour. Transfer them to a zip-top bag or airtight container, and freeze them for up to two months. Thaw them overnight in the fridge before enjoying them.

Your chocolate may not be smooth for a few reasons. The first is you may have burned it in the microwave. When you burn chocolate, it will seize and become clumpy. Unfortunately, this is unfixable. It’s also possible that you left out the shortening. Shortening makes the chocolate slightly less viscous, which makes it easier to evenly coat the truffles. It also makes it smooth and glossy. Don’t skip this ingredient!

To help puppy chow balls hold their shape, be sure to use a no-stir creamy peanut butter. It’s much thicker than the natural peanut butters you have to stir. Because their oils separate so easily, natural peanut butters will make the mixture softer and more malleable.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6513. I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off. And contestants have seriously struggled with it over the years. But according to Paul Hollywood, this season’s challenge featuring blue cheese and roasted grape flatbreads was the worst yet. After 60 minutes of kneading, grape-roasting, and undercooking, the bakers produced trays of thick, raw flatbreads that Paul and Nigella could barely eat.

After bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul said, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings. The popular opinion? The bakers were set up to fail—and also that the flavors seemed a little weird.

With all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself. While I purposefully did NOT watch the episode before my attempt, I did print the full recipe from the GBBO website. This recipe was definitely WAY more helpful than the one the bakers were given, and I followed it to the letter.

Here’s how it went: the good, the bad, and the very ugly.

The beginning? Very smooth. I put the grapes in the oven (the online recipe told me to roast them as a whole bunch rather than cutting them up) and made the bread dough, kneading it for the five minutes specified before letting it rest.

As soon as I set the dough aside to rest, I discovered how absolutely torturous technical downtime is. I was at an absolute loss. I had nothing to do…except read the recipe over and over again and make sure I knew what 8 cm and 23 cm looked like.

Interestingly enough, the bakers on the show didn’t have this downtime; they were busy cutting and roasting their grapes by then. That said, I don’t think that order was necessarily better; with the time spent slicing the grapes, they wouldn’t have had much time at ALL to roast—and not nearly enough to cool.

The grapes came out of the oven. They weren’t very roasted—as one of the bakers said, they just looked like “raw grapes”—but the recipe said 20 minutes and gave no indicators for how roasted they should be (and also I knew they needed to cool before stuffing), so I just went with it.

I dumped out the dough (a rude awakening after its 15-minute rest) and chopped it into eight pieces. Immediately, I realized I should have weighed the larger ball and divided it by eight so I could make sure all the pieces were equal, but I didn’t have much time to fuss, so I tried to make them roughly the same weight and moved on.

The recipe said to roll out each portion of dough into an 8 cm circle, fill it with five roasted grapes and one-eighth of the blue cheese, lift the edges of the circle up to pinch them together, then turn the little ball seam side down and roll the whole thing out into a 23 cm circle.

To begin, I cut my dough into wedges from the larger ball, and it was hard to roll them out into a circle to fill. But that was nothing compared to the problems I had rolling out the filled dough. First, the dough wasn’t rested enough, so it kept springing back at me as I tried to roll it out. But the bigger issue was the grapes. Since they were still pretty juicy, they started bursting as I rolled out the flatbread, flying to the edges and tearing holes in the dough as they oozed out.

After over 15 minutes of stuffing and rolling, my workstation was littered with burst grape guts. None of my flatbreads were 23 cm wide (I think the widest they got was 18?) and I still had three to roll out, but I also knew I needed to start cooking or I was going to have eight totally raw flatbreads at the end of time.

Cooking the flatbreads wasn’t a total disaster—I guess—but grape juice oozed out of the holes where they burst and left black patches of burnt sugar on the pan, which I had absolutely no time to clean out since I was still racing the clock. Fortunately, the flatbreads didn’t seem to need the full 90 seconds per side. In fact, they seemed to need constant attention to prevent them from burning, which was bad news since I was still trying to roll out the remaining three flatbreads on the side.

Time was up, and I had five cooked (burst) stuffed flatbreads on my sheet tray, three totally raw ones on the countertop, and a smoking pan. I now know how the bakers feel at the end of such challenges: slightly insane and utterly defeated.

Looking back on the challenge, I can honestly say that it was difficult and somewhat impossible. Ultimately, I couldn’t get all the flatbreads cooked in time, even though I was rolling them out much thinner than the bakers were. But while timing was definitely a problem, the bigger issue was the impossible stupidity of stuffing juicy grapes inside a flatbread and then trying to roll it out without the grapes bursting out and ruining the dough.

Since I managed to cook five flatbreads, I could (unlike Paul and Nigella) taste the finished result—but honestly, I wasn’t a fan. The blue cheese was WAY too strong, and the grapes felt like random pockets of juice in an otherwise savory flatbread. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend trying this challenge yourself—unless you want to be scrubbing the burnt bits of grape sugar off your pan for the next week.

#6512. Thanksgiving Leftovers Nachos

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

These Thanksgiving leftovers nachos are piled high with turkey, Brie, stuffing and squash before being finished with gravy, cranberry sauce and French-fried onions.

Scouring the internet in search of ideas for what to make with your Thanksgiving leftovers? While turkey potpie and the infamous Moist Maker sandwich from Friends are always solid choices, I implore you to try Thanksgiving leftovers nachos this year.

If you spend any time on social media, this likely isn’t the first recipe for Thanksgiving leftovers nachos you’ve seen. But I promise it’s the best. Our rendition begins with a pile of corn tortilla chips layered with leftover roast turkey and a secret ingredient: creamy Brie cheese. Next, leftover stuffing and roasted butternut squash (or candied sweet potatoes) are piled on before the nachos bake to crispy, cheesy perfection. Once finished with turkey gravy, cranberry sauce, and a shower of French-fried onions and herbs, this mountain of Thanksgiving glory is a feast for the senses.

Serve these Thanksgiving leftovers nachos after a day of Black Friday shopping, or invite friends over for the big game on Sunday afternoon. Absolutely no one will complain about a second Thanksgiving in nacho form.

Preheat the oven to 400°F. In separate microwave-safe containers, reheat the leftover turkey, squash and stuffing until they’re warmed through.

On a 15x10x1-inch baking sheet, arrange a layer of tortilla chips. Top them with half of the cubed Brie and shredded turkey. Repeat with another layer of chips, Brie and turkey.

Crumble the stuffing over the nachos, then top with the roasted butternut squash. Bake the nachos until the cheese is melted and the toppings are heated through, about 10 to 12 minutes.

While the nachos bake, warm the gravy in the microwave or on the stovetop until it’s heated through.

Drizzle the nachos with warm gravy, dollop small spoonfuls of cranberry sauce on top, and sprinkle them with fresh herbs and French-fried onions. Serve the nachos with additional cranberry sauce and gravy on the side.

Thanksgiving leftovers nachos are best enjoyed immediately. Since they’re piled high with toppings and warm gravy, the chips will get soggy when stored. For best results, make only what you intend to eat in one sitting.

Tortilla chips will almost always soften a bit when they’re baked as nachos. You can slow the process, however, by selecting thicker, sturdier chips that hold up to the weight and moisture of the nacho toppings. Here are our favorite tortilla chip brands that will stand up to the task.

You may also wish to bake the chips briefly for three to five minutes before piling on the toppings. Warming the chips first drives out any residual moisture and boosts their moisture resistance.

Not really. While the ingredient amounts in the recipe offer the best ratios of flavor and texture (in our opinion), you can wing it and use whatever leftovers you have on hand. These nachos will taste sublime no matter what.

These nachos are pretty spectacular—so much so that you may find yourself craving them long after Thanksgiving has passed and there are no leftovers in sight. While you would have to prepare a miniature holiday dinner to make these nachos, you can simplify things by using a box of stovetop stuffing, precut butternut squash (for easy roasting), canned cranberries and rotisserie chicken instead of turkey.

This an all-in-one meal that doesn’t need any sides. That said, there’s always room for a fun cocktail. Cranberry margaritas are another great Mexican-Thanksgiving mashup. Looking for dessert? If you have leftover pumpkin puree, make pumpkin bars for a quick and easy treat. Of course, you may also have leftover Thanksgiving desserts to continue chipping away at, too.

#6511. Andy Baraghani's Ditto Café Is His Most Personal Project Yet

Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

He lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are currently splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel important. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

“Oh,” he says casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a New York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani announced he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”

His background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”

Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he says it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

Now, though, Baraghani says he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

“There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.)

Literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in New York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

The goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the plan is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.)

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he says simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

And for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

#6509. This Is What Christmas Dinner Would Look Like in ‘A Christmas Carol’

I'll give you Mr. Scrooge, the Founder of the Feast! Here are all the foods Charles Dickens wrote about in A Christmas Carol.

Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol occupies a particularly important place in my heart. My grandma gifted me her copy when I was in junior high, and I’ve returned to it nearly every Christmas since, each year finding something in the story that speaks to me in a new way.

And although I’m generally suspicious of film adaptations of the books I love, there are two versions I treasure every bit as much as the original story. I fell in love with them as a child, probably around the same time. The first was The Muppet Christmas Carol, which combined two of my favorite things: the Muppets and jaunty show tunes. I watched it incessantly throughout the Christmas season, and the tradition has carried on with my own children, who now know every song and every word of dialogue.

The other was the 1984 adaptation starring George C. Scott. I love its surreal, slightly unsettling atmosphere, the magnificent strangeness of the Ghost of Christmas Present and the genuinely frightening revelation of Ignorance and Want. And after all that darkness, Scrooge’s redemption is almost unbearably moving.

With another film adaptation arriving this year (Ebenezer), it’s clear that Dickens’s masterpiece has kept its hold on us. And because the food is an enormous part of what makes the story’s celebrations so memorable, I wanted to take a closer look at the happy commotion of the Cratchits’ kitchen, Fezziwig’s Christmas party and the astonishing abundance surrounding the Ghost of Christmas Present. Nearly two centuries later, those descriptions still give us a remarkably complete picture of what Christmas tasted like in Dickens’s world.

The Cratchits’ Christmas goose is one of the most eagerly anticipated meals in literature. As the family busies itself with the accompaniments, the younger children can hardly contain their excitement. When Mrs. Cratchit finally brings the bird to the table, Dickens describes it arriving with a great flourish and the stuffing spilling out as it’s carved.

Goose was a traditional Christmas centerpiece in Victorian England, particularly for families who couldn’t afford a turkey. Its rich, dark meat was well-suited to roasting, and sage-and-onion stuffing was a familiar accompaniment.

Bob declares that no goose has ever been so tender and delicious, and the family agrees wholeheartedly. The bird may be small for so many people, but the family’s excitement is anything but.

While the goose roasts, the Cratchit household is busy! Peter tends to the mashed potatoes, Belinda sweetens the apple sauce, and Mrs. Cratchit prepares the gravy. Nearly two centuries later, the menu would look perfectly at home on a modern Christmas table.

Apple sauce was an especially good companion to roast goose, with its tart sweetness balancing the bird’s rich, fatty meat. The mashed potatoes and gravy rounded out the meal, providing plenty of comfort alongside the centerpiece.

For all his considerable literary talents, Charles Dickens also had a good understanding of the anxiety that comes with serving a dessert you’re not entirely sure has turned out.

While Mrs. Cratchit retrieves her Christmas plum pudding from the kitchen, the family imagines every possible disaster. Perhaps it isn’t cooked through, or perhaps it will break when she turns it out. The younger children even worry that someone might have stolen it. Fortunately, Mrs. Cratchit returns triumphant with a pudding Dickens describes as a “speckled cannon-ball,” blazing with brandy and decorated with holly.

Traditionally, plum pudding was a dense mixture of dried fruit, suet, spices and other ingredients, boiled for hours in a cloth. Despite the name, it didn’t necessarily contain plums; the term was historically used for dried fruits such as raisins.

Bob declares the pudding Mrs. Cratchit’s greatest success since their marriage, and nobody dreams of disagreeing. The pudding may be modest in size, but to the Cratchits, it’s a triumph, and Mrs. Cratchit deserves every word of their praise.

Few characters in A Christmas Carol embody the spirit of Christmas quite like old Mr. Fezziwig. When the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge back to the Christmas party hosted by his former employer, we’re treated to a lively evening of dancing, music, laughter and an impressive assortment of refreshments, including mince pies.

These little pastries had been associated with English Christmas celebrations for generations. Earlier versions of mincemeat often contained actual meat alongside dried fruit, suet and spices. By Dickens’s time, sweeter fillings were increasingly common, though meat hadn’t disappeared from every recipe.

I rather like imagining Fezziwig presiding over the festivities, dispensing good cheer as generously as the food. His party is one of the few memories that briefly softens Scrooge, and it’s easy to understand why.

After the Cratchit family finishes dinner, apples and oranges are brought out, chestnuts are placed on the fire, and Bob serves a warm drink of gin and lemon. With the excitement of the goose and Christmas pudding behind them, the family settles in for the evening.

Roasted chestnuts were a familiar winter treat in Victorian London, sold hot by street vendors and enjoyed at home. Oranges were especially welcome during the winter months, when fresh fruit was less readily available.

Dickens mentions that the family has only two tumblers and a custard cup without a handle, a detail I love for its specificity. The bustle of dinner has given way to the quieter pleasure of sitting together, and Dickens allows us to linger with the family a little longer before the evening draws to a close.

Christmas celebrations in Dickens’s England didn’t necessarily end on Dec. 25. Twelfth Night, traditionally observed on Jan. 5 or 6, marked the close of the Twelve Days of Christmas, often with a party and an elaborate cake. Twelfth cakes were rich with dried fruit and spices, beautifully decorated and sometimes baked with a hidden bean. Whoever found the bean in their slice might be crowned king or queen of the festivities, an arrangement that presumably made everyone a little more attentive to their dessert.

Dickens details “immense twelfth-cakes” among the extraordinary foods surrounding the Ghost of Christmas Present. The tradition was already evolving by 1843, but the cakes were still familiar enough to belong on his magnificent collection of Christmas indulgences.

Dickens includes entire barrels of oysters among the Ghost of Christmas Present’s holiday foods, which may seem an extravagant addition to modern readers.

In Victorian London, though, oysters were commonly eaten, including by working-class people. They were sold by street vendors, served in taverns and prepared in everything from pies to stews. Britain’s oyster fisheries were once enormously productive, although overharvesting and pollution eventually led to their decline.

Dickens’s Ghost certainly had no shortage of delights surrounding him, but the barrels of oysters wouldn’t necessarily have struck his readers as the most impressive things in the room.

When Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning and realizes he’s been given another chance, one of his first acts is to purchase an enormous turkey for the Cratchits.

He sends a boy to the poulterer’s shop for the prize bird, giddy at the thought of how surprised the family will be. Dickens describes Scrooge’s delight so vividly that it’s difficult not to share his excitement.

Roast turkey was becoming fashionable for Christmas dinner in Victorian England, particularly among wealthier households. Compared with the Cratchits’ modest goose, Scrooge’s gift is a magnificent extravagance.

I especially love that he arranges for the bird to be delivered anonymously. He’s discovered the joy of doing something generous without expecting anything in return, and he can barely contain himself.

At the end of the story, Scrooge promises Bob Cratchit a raise and suggests they discuss the particulars over a bowl of smoking bishop. It’s a peculiar name for what was essentially a warm, spiced wine punch.

Smoking bishop was traditionally prepared with red wine or port, roasted citrus, sugar and spices. The ingredients were warmed together to make a fragrant cocktail similar to modern mulled wine. It belonged to a family of similarly named punches, including smoking cardinal and smoking pope. Victorian drinkers evidently enjoyed a little ecclesiastical creativity with their beverages.

I love that Dickens saves this particular drink for the end. We’ve seen the Cratchits gather around their modest dinner and the Ghost of Christmas Present preside over a feast of extraordinary abundance. Now Scrooge, who once wanted nothing to do with either, is inviting Bob Cratchit to share a bowl of punch. Of all the wonderful things on Dickens’s Christmas menu, that invitation may be the most satisfying.

#6508. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6504. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

Adapted from Chaat: Recipes from the Kitchens, Markets, and Railways of India by Maneet Chauhan and Jody Eddy. Copyright © 2020. Available from Clarkson Potter.

#6503. The Exiled Thanksgiving Dishes You Forgot Were Once on the Table

There was a time when Thanksgiving dinner involved gelatin—and lots of it.

Thanksgiving is a holiday that doesn’t take kindly to change. Suggest replacing the mashed potatoes or leaving the stuffing off the menu, and you’re likely to hear about it until Easter. Yet for all our devotion to tradition, the Thanksgiving table has changed quite a bit over the years. Somewhere along the way, entire dishes disappeared, and most of us barely noticed.

Some were beloved family favorites that gradually fell out of fashion. Others were products of an era when gelatin was considered an essential ingredient, even in dishes that had no business holding that much shape. Looking through old Thanksgiving menus, cookbooks and holiday advertisements reveals a rather wonderful assortment of foods that once had a place alongside the turkey. A few deserve to come back. Others might be better left to history, although I would very much like to meet the people responsible for them.

“Aspic” is a lovely word. It’s French, sophisticated, and just mysterious enough to suggest that whatever arrives at the table will be very impressive. You could put it on a formal dinner menu and nobody would think twice. But what you’re actually discussing is meat Jell-O.

And not some unfortunate kitchen experiment, either. Savory aspics were perfectly respectable additions to holiday meals well into the 1950s, with suspensions of meat, vegetables, seafood and even hard-boiled eggs presented in elaborate molds. The finished creations could be sliced into neat portions, allowing guests to admire every carefully arranged ingredient through a translucent wall of solidified broth.

There’s something almost admirable about the confidence required to make one of these. Imagine spending hours arranging shrimp and vegetables in a decorative mold, then carrying it proudly to the dining room as though everyone had been waiting all year for a slice of cold, wobbly meat.

Not every gelatin creation merits as harsh a judgment as aspic. I have a certain affection for the brightly colored Jell-O salads that used to appear at holiday gatherings. There was something cheerful about a ruby-red cranberry gelatin salad or a fluffy lime concoction studded with pineapple, even if calling either one a “salad” required a fairly generous interpretation of the word.

These dishes were enormously popular in the mid-20th century, when molded gelatin desserts offered home cooks an opportunity to get creative with fruit, nuts, cream cheese, whipped topping and whatever else happened to be in the refrigerator. Some combinations were genuinely delicious. Others involved shredded carrots, celery or mayonnaise, at which point the distinction between salad and practical joke became rather difficult to maintain.

I’d happily make room for a cranberry Jell-O salad at Thanksgiving. The ones made with canned tuna can remain in retirement.

There was a time, particularly in the 1890s, when mincemeat pie was every bit as deserving of a place on the Thanksgiving dessert table as pumpkin or apple pie. Its rich filling of dried fruits, spices and citrus had a long history in English cooking, and early versions also contained actual meat—often beef or mutton—along with suet.

The meat gradually disappeared from many recipes, leaving behind the sweet, deeply spiced filling that became a holiday tradition in its own right. Even so, the name has never done the pie any favors. Tell someone you’re serving mincemeat for dessert, and there’s a reasonable chance they’ll assume you’ve been sampling too many Thanksgiving cocktails.

That’s a shame, because a well-made mincemeat pie has plenty going for it, particularly for anyone who loves the warm flavors of cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg. It may be a harder sell than pumpkin pie, but I wouldn’t object to seeing it make a modest comeback.

Waldorf salad has much more glamorous origins than most other dishes on this list. It was created at New York’s Waldorf Hotel in the 1890s, originally as a simple combination of apples, celery and mayonnaise. Walnuts became a familiar addition later, and by the 1960s, the salad had found its way onto holiday tables across the country.

I can understand why. The crisp apples and celery provide a welcome contrast to the rich, heavy dishes that make up Thanksgiving dinner, while the walnuts add enough substance to make it feel like more than just a bowl of chopped fruit. It’s refreshing, pleasantly crunchy and especially good alongside roasted turkey.

Of all the dishes that have slipped off the Thanksgiving menu, Waldorf salad might be one of the easiest to bring back. It requires very little fuss, and a fresh, crisp side is hardly unwelcome at a table already crowded with casseroles.

At some point in the ’50s, we became convinced that nearly every food could be improved by pressing it into a loaf pan.

The holiday vegetable loaf was one expression of that enthusiasm, turning assorted vegetables into a tidy, sliceable centerpiece with the help of binders like eggs, breadcrumbs or gelatin. Some versions were baked, while others emerged cold from the refrigerator, ready to be unmolded and presented with considerable ceremony.

I understand the practical appeal of preparing a dish ahead of time, particularly for Thanksgiving. What I struggle to understand is the insistence that vegetables should be made to resemble meatloaf. Carrots, peas and green beans are perfectly capable of sharing a serving dish without being pressed into a rectangular block.

Hot Dr Pepper sounds like something you’d find in a cookbook published during a national shortage of good judgment. But it was a genuine promotional idea, introduced by Dr Pepper in the 1960s as a way to enjoy the soft drink in colder weather.

The instructions were simple: Heat Dr Pepper, pour it into a mug and add a thin slice of lemon. The company promoted it as a warming drink for winter gatherings, making it an intriguing candidate for the sort of holiday refreshment that now seems to have vanished almost completely.

I can’t decide whether this is a terrible idea or one that deserves a fair trial. Dr Pepper already has a distinctive blend of sweet and spicy flavors, and warm spiced drinks are hardly unusual during the holidays. The lemon is an interesting touch, too. I wouldn’t necessarily replace the hot apple cider, but curiosity might get the better of me.

There are questionable vintage recipes, and then there are the recipes that suggest the author had finally snapped. Cranberry mayonnaise candles belong firmly in the second category.

The idea was to turn cranberry sauce and mayonnaise into a molded holiday creation resembling a candle, complete with a decorative wick or flame effect depending on the version. It was the sort of elaborate presentation that food companies once promoted with an entirely straight face, apparently confident that a candle-shaped mixture of fruit and mayonnaise was just what the Thanksgiving feast had been missing.

I have several questions, beginning with why the cranberry sauce needed to look like a candle and ending with why mayonnaise was invited to the party. There’s also the matter of placing something resembling a candle in the food and expecting guests to understand they’re supposed to eat it.

If you’ve ever wondered what to do with leftover turkey, the sensible answers include sandwiches, soups, potpies and perhaps casseroles. Vintage recipe developers, however, were not always interested in sensible answers.

Enter frozen jellied turkey vegetable salad, a 1970s creation that manages to combine several questionable ideas into a single dish. Turkey, vegetables and a gelatin-based mixture were assembled into a cold, molded preparation that was perhaps more ambitious than necessary.

It’s difficult to imagine anyone looking at a plate of leftover turkey and deciding that what it really needed was to become a frozen, sliceable salad. Yet recipes like this reflect a period when casserole popsicles made perfect sense.

Creamed pearl onions were a familiar sight on Thanksgiving tables in the 1920s, and I think we may have been too quick to let them go. Tender little onions in a rich, buttery cream sauce are exactly the sort of thing that belongs alongside roast turkey, mashed potatoes and stuffing. They’re comforting, a little old-fashioned, and wonderfully suited to a holiday when nobody is particularly concerned about their butter intake.

They also have the advantage of feeling special without requiring an elaborate presentation. Peeling a mountain of tiny onions is admittedly nobody’s idea of holiday fun, but frozen pearl onions make the whole business much easier. If your family has never had creamed onions at Thanksgiving, this may be a tradition worth borrowing from an earlier generation.

#6502. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6501. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6500. I Tried to Get a McDonald’s Pokemon Happy Meal, and It Wasn’t Total Chaos

Despite the rumors I had heard about long lines and purchase limits, the new Pokemon Happy Meal was easier to get (and more adorable) than I thought.

When my son came home from summer camp a few years ago with a small pack of gifted Pokemon cards and a new hobby, I had no idea what lay ahead. Very quickly, locating Pokemon cards on shelves changed from finding them behind the register for a slightly higher price to not being able to find them at all. A renewed interest in collecting Pokemon cards has made everything Pokemon hotter than ever. And, somehow, I became a Poke-person.

Unwilling to pay (high) market price, my son and I have joined long lines before stores open to try and get cards. I’ve seen frenzied parents, kids and scalpers hoping to nab hard-to-find collections. One time the police were called on potential line-jumpers. So, when I heard McDonald’s Pokemon Happy Meals were coming, I had no idea if I’d be able to purchase one or if they were going to sell out immediately. I’m too deep into the world of Pokemon not to try, and what shocked me the most was how simple it was!

A McDonald’s Pokemon Happy Meal is a regular Happy Meal housed in one of three Pokemon-themed boxes, though sadly ours was in a regular red box. Each meal has a small box with one of 15 Pokemon toys and two cards. There are 15 cards in this promotion, and seven of them have shiny foil holographic elements. Each toy features a Pokemon character in the shape of a mini Happy Meal. It has a hinged plastic clip on the back so you can attach it to a bag or flip it up and use it as a card holder. The meal also had unexpectedly fun pouches of Pokemon-designed apple slices.

Some websites claimed that during the five-week promotion, there would be specific Pokemon toys allotted for each week, but if that was the plan, it’s already off track. We received two Pokemon that were supposedly marked for week three, and various Poke-loving social media posts showed off photos with an assortment of all 15 characters.

Before the launch, there was speculation that Pokemon Happy Meals would be limited to one per customer or potentially sold only if a child was present, in an effort to fight scalpers. I couldn’t find anything official from McDonald’s or Pokemon Center on this policy, and it wasn’t my experience. When I ordered with my son, we asked for two, and there was no mention of limits. The solo woman behind me ordered without issue.

The line at my local McDonald’s was long, but mostly because we headed there right after school, when plenty of hungry teenagers were there. I saw only a few other people opening Pokemon toys, so for all the buzz around this collab, it was my easiest Pokemon experience in years.

Pokemon Happy Meals will be available in the U.S. until Dec. 14. However, the most important thing to remember is that this promotion is while supplies last. Considering that reseller sites like eBay are already buzzing with toys and cards, there is a good chance supplies will sell out before then.

Even though our fries were cold, the toys are adorable, and the art on the cards is Poke-perfection. I don’t think we will catch them all, but hopefully we can get a few more while they are available.

Will you be trying to collect one or all of the toys and cards? Let us know in the comments!

#6499. Chatpata Potato Chip Tower

Cookbook author Rachel Gurjar doesn’t usually jump on food trends, but the potato chip tower called to her. “Chips are already great as is, but I knew a version inspired by chana chor—a fiery street snack made from flattened, fried black chickpeas tossed with onions, chiles, lemon, and chaat masala—would kick it up a notch,” she writes in her debut title, East to East. Chatpata is a Hindi word that means salty, sour, spicy, and sweet at the same time, and this chatpata potato chip tower absolutely lives up to its name. While you can use any potato chips you like—or even substitute tortilla chips, pita chips, or fried pita bread—Gurjar recommends thick kettle-cooked chips, as they stay crispy longer.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

#6497. I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

One of these could've used a few extra sauce packets.

I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a new FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

There were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

You've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

#6496. Too Busy for Breakfast? Make These Pumpkin Overnight Oats

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

Yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “important,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

On a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most important meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

#6495. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.
