#6485. Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

Another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

New in this update: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included)

This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” says senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

Performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

The Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate."

What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included)

Amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

In testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as quickly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

What we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively quickly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

What we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

In testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

This is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time.

We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor).

This Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform and handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls). I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners. I ultimately didn’t feel its performance merited its price tag, which is more than double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing.

True to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That said, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily.

This rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons.

The Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale.

MyWeigh KD-8000 Bakers Math Kitchen Scale

This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill.

At less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee.

This scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali.

This scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue.

Joseph Joseph TriScale Compact Folding Digital Kitchen Food Scale

Like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That said, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons.

I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and big platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams.

KitchenAid Dual Platform Digital Kitchen Scale

We noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The big scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight.

Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more important, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of said ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight.

ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale

I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out quickly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

To use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

Baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

Alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

#6484. Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing. That was a very impressive way to bypass the restrictions imposed by rocket fairings. But that's not practical in every case.

What's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there. That's what NOM4D, the Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design program is demonstrating. NOM4D reached an important milestone recently when it successfully demonstrated automated in-space assembly for the first time.

The demonstration involved a gantry robot, also known as a linear robot, building a typical truss structure. Gantry robots move in straight lines along x, y, and z axes. The payload came from Caltech and consisted of individual components with custom joints put together to form the structure. The individual components were not only assembled, but a thin reflective mesh that mimics what a space-based antenna might have was also simultaneously applied.

âNOM4Dâs objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space,â said Andrew Detor, NOM4D program manager. âBy âvery large,â I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.â

This concept image shows a space-based antenna autonomously assembled by a NOM4D-type device. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

There is no shortage of ideas of how space-based manufacturing and construction could be used, but it all starts with programs like NOM4D. NOM4D is fairly simple at this point, like a child's construction toy, but that's its strength.

âYou can think of the Caltech approach as similar to Tinkertoys or Kânex construction toys: individual truss members are joined at nodes, one section at a time, to create a larger structure,â Detor said. âWithin the automated assembly box, each section is built piece by piece, a reflective mesh is attached, and the assembled sections are deployed as they are complete. There are no complicated robotics or advanced algorithms; itâs just solid engineering from the Caltech team to combine operations in a way that scales.â

Decades ago, thinkers proposed different types of rotating space stations that could be homes for thousands of people. The O'Neill Cylinder is probably the most well-known one of these, and space-heads and sci-fi dreamers of a certain age may have carried around a dog-eared copy of Gerard K. O'Neill's "The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space."

"More important than material issues, I think there is reason to hope that the opening of a new, high frontier will challenge the best that is in us, that the new lands waiting to be built in space will give us new freedom to search for better governments, social systems, and ways of life, and that our children may thereby find a world richer in opportunity by our efforts during the decades ahead," O'Neill wrote.

The O'Neill Cylinder lies in the realm of science fiction or the distant future for now, as do O'Neill's hopes for humanity. But that was 50 years ago, and technology has advanced considerably, even if how humans conduct themselves hasn't advanced at the same pace.

But there are other proposed space structures that are closer to reality, and they may be stages towards O'Neill's hopeful vision that can be built by NOM4D or its successor.

It may begin with Low-Earth Orbit transfer stations and lunar orbit stations that would expand our presence in space. The proposed Lunar Gateway was one of these, and was envisioned as a modular design built in space from pre-made components. It would be a docking station and communications relay facility for trips to the lunar surface and operations there. These types of orbital facilities could be hybrids of pre-made components and structural frameworks made by NOM4D or something like it.

This concept image shows how a NOM4D-inspired device might autonomously construct a circular truss structure in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

Another future use for scalable construction concerns lunar lava tubes. The Moon has what appear to be networks of subsurface lava tubes that provide natural protection from hazards. Robotic assembly could feasibly be used to reinforce these natural tubes and turn them into habitats.

Another idea is liquid mirror telescopes. Building a huge telescope mirror and sending it into space would be near impossible, but a liquid mirror telescope could be built in a lunar crater out of components shipped individually into space. And NASA's Lunar Crater Radio Telescope (LCRT) is a concept for a crater-based telescope on the lunar far side, isolated from Earth's radio pollution. These ideas are waiting for the engineering to catch up.

âIn a future space economy, weâre going to need large things,â Detor said. âThink large space depots or habitats, large solar arrays to collect power, or large radio antennas to explore the edges of the universe. Those things require size, and NOM4D gives us a path to accelerate creation of new capabilities.â

The rapid advancement of the NOM4D program surprised even NOM4D personnel themselves. This successful on-orbit demonstration wasn't expected to happen so soon.

Back in February 2025, NOM4D changed its timeline. What was expected to be a third phase of more laboratory tests was instead changed to on-orbit tests, and SpaceX launched Caltech's NOM4D payload into space in March 2026.

âCaltech [California Institute of Technology] and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have demonstrated tremendous advances in the first two phases and have now partnered in Phase 3 with space-launch companies to conduct in-space testing of their novel assembly processes and materials,â Detor said at the time. âOriginally, Phase 3 was going to be about making things more precisely in the lab than we did in Phase 2. But we said, âYou know, the maturity is there, and there would be more impact if we took the capabilities we have now and actually go demonstrate them in space to show that it can be done,â"Detor said.

Now, way ahead of its original schedule, NOM4D has demonstrated its capabilities and is maturing rapidly. As Detor makes clear, leaping from the laboratory to space is a huge jump.

âItâs the speed and the scale that made this a DARPA project. We went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype into space in 15 months,â Detor said. âOperating in space is much harder than operating on the ground â thereâs virtually no margin to address issues that may arise. Testing in the operational environment is instrumental to rapidly maturing the technology.â

There's still another test upcoming for NOM4D now that it's demonstrated successful on-orbit assembly. Next, the NOM4D team from University of Illinois Urbana-Champagne will launch a test project to the ISS. This will be more than just assembly; it will demonstrate composite material processing. A monomer resin will be used to build a high-strength structure in space. It will use an energy-efficient method to heat the resin and create a strong polymer. This is similar to how resins are used in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) manufacturing to build things like aerospace components, where strength and light weight are critical.

If that test is successful, then it really will be time to start thinking big, according to Detor.

This concept image shows what the future of NOM4D-like construction might look like. Large space structures like these could be built entirely in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

âThe NOM4D Caltech demonstration is not an endpoint; itâs a beginning,â Detor said. âNow that weâve demonstrated a process that can scale to large structures, what do we go make? What wild ideas get assembled thousands of miles above us and what new capabilities do those structures enable?â

Is it time to open Gerard K. O'Neill's seminal book again?

The O'Neill Cylinder, the OG of space habitats. Maybe one day. Image Credit: By NASA/Rick Guidice - https://space.nss.org/settlement/nasa/70sArtHiRes/70sArt/art.html (image link), Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=675434

#6483. Mexican Seafood and Natural Wines Are in the Spotlight at This New NYC Restaurant

A stacked tuna tostada, puckering shrimp aguachile, and more seafood dishes stun at El Camarón Peludo

Known for their roasted and slow-cooked meats at Taqueria Ramirez, Tania Apolinar and Giovanni Cervantes partnered with chef Carlos Barrera to open a new seafood-focused wine bar this year. Here’s what a full day of prep looks like at El Camarón Peludo in the West Village.

First, fresh shrimp from Sinaloa, Mexico; Ecuador; and more locales are de-shelled and de-veined for three central shrimp dishes. Then, Cervantes starts the fresh salsa for the day, taste testing and comparing each batch to the salsa from last week to make sure the flavor is consistent. A bright red salsa is mixed with mayo to create the sauce on the camarones zarandeados, a shrimp version of a fish dish from the Pacific coast of Mexico that is usually grilled in a flat wire grill basket.

Upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

Back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

Watch the team at the Mexican seafood wine bar prepare tostadas, tacos, and flavor-packed aguachile in the newest episode of Now Open.

#6482. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

#6481. Planets Don't Just Disappear, But They Can Wobble Out of Sight if Their Neighbour is Close Enough

NASA's TESS mission was a success by almost any measure. So far, as of mid-October 2026, it's identified more than 8,100 candidate exoplanets, and just over 1,000 of them have been confirmed. The mission is still ongoing, and astronomers are also finding more exoplanets in its archival data with new machine learning techniques.

TESS was primarily aimed at finding smaller super-Earths and sub-Neptunes, but it also found many hot-Jupiters during its mission. One of them, about 1,000 light years away, is a hot Jupiter named TOI-2535b and it exhibited some strange behaviour. TESS observed multiple transits by TOI-2535b over seven years, then the planet seemed to just disappear.

Planets can't just disappear, unless the Death Star is nearby, and astronomers have wondered what's behind the hot Jupiter's disappearing act. New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has a natural explanation for the vanished star. It's titled "A TESS Disappearing Act: The Vanishing Transits of TOI-2535 b," and the corresponding author is Samuel Yee, a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA.

"Planetary transits require a fortuitous alignment between a planetâs orbit and our line of sight, but dynamical interactions can render this geometric coincidence only temporary," the authors write in their research letter. "We report the discovery of the hot Jupiter TOI-2535b, the first confirmed planet orbiting a single star whose transits have been directly observed to disappear."

Detecting planets via the transit method only works if everything lines up, as the authors explain. But everything doesn't necessarily stay lined up. Dynamical interactions abound in solar systems, as we know from our own Solar System's history. Giant planets have migrated, ending old, stable orbital patterns and heralding new ones. Interactions can scatter smaller objects, and even send comets careening into the inner Solar System.

But a massive shift isn't required to upset the finely-tuned line of sight that allows us to see distant exoplanets as they transit their stars.

"Because a planet is only observed to transit when its orbit normal is within a few degrees of the sky plane, even small changes in a planetâs orbital inclination can result in measurable changes in its transit shape," the authors explain. "For sufficiently large inclination changes, a planet may only have the correct transit geometry for a fraction of its dynamical evolution."

Here's the kicker: "If the variation is fast enough and we are lucky to catch the planet in the right phase of its inclination evolution, we may see its transits appear or disappear," the researchers write.

This figure presents some of the research's findings. The first panel shows TESS transits from sectors 10, 63, and 90. Sectors are rectangular strips of the sky that TESS observes. The second panel shows the movement of the transit chord across the stellar disk. The dark circle shows TOI-2535b's size relative to its star. Image Credit: Samuel W. Yee et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L60

That's what happened with TOI-2535b, according to this work, and it's probably because of another exoplanet interacting with the hot Jupiter.

By watching it over several years, astronomers observed TOI-2535b's orbit in detail. It didn't just suddenly disappear. Both the timing and the shape of the transit slowly changed.

This can happen with circumbinary exoplanets, those that orbit a binary star. "Circumbinary planets frequently exhibit rapid changes in their transit impact parameters," the authors write. "As a result, even a small misalignment between the two orbits leads to intervals when the planet may transit both, one, or neither of its host stars."

But TOI-2535b orbits a single star, making its disappearance extremely unusual. "Around single stars, inclination variations of planets are typically less dramatic and appear to be relatively rare," the researchers explain. But that's what seems to be happening here due to the influence of another exoplanet.

âWe think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but thatâs not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each otherâs orbits. We know of a few systems that are like this,â said Yee. âThis is the most extreme example weâve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly. The planetâs orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.â

This work rests partly on what are called Transit Duration Variations (TDV). These are small yet measurable and periodic changes in the amount of time it takes for an exoplanet to complete a transit in front of its star. TOI-2535b's TDVs are unusual, according to the authors, and so are the changes in its orbital inclination.

"The TOI-2535 system is an unusual and exceptional system in many ways. Observationally, it has the largest TDVs and inclination change ever observed for a planet orbiting a single star, with a precession period of decades, shorter than other known systems," the authors explain. The system also has some of the largest Transit Timing Variations (TTVs) ever detected, and they're definitely the largest ever detected for a hot Jupiter.

The researchers say that another, neighbouring exoplanet of Saturn-mass or greater is tugging on the exoplanet's orbit, making it "disappear." This is surprising, since hot Jupiter's aren't expected to have any close neighbours. In the rare cases where they do have neighbours, the neighbours are quite a bit less massive.

"This makes TOI-2535b one of only a handful of hot Jupiters known to have a close-by planetary companion. Furthermore, the companion to TOI-2535b is likely a second short-period giant planet. This differs from all but one of the currently known hot Jupiters with a nearby companion, in which the companions are sub-Neptunes or super-Earths," the authors write.

A pair of massive gas giants orbiting one system in resonance with each other isn't something planet-formation models predict. The authors rule out high-eccentricity migration as a cause. "Such systems could not have formed through high-eccentricity migration, which has been posited to be responsible for most other hot Jupiters," the authors write. But there are two other migration possibilities.

In one, the planet is pulled into an eccentric orbit by a powerful interaction of some sort, possibly a near collision with another object, and then the star's gravity pulls it in, where it takes up residence as a hot Jupiter.

The second scenario sees the planet pulled into the inner solar system with other planets inside the protoplanetary disk. But that counterindicates the observed orbital tilts. "However, the protoplanetary disk would also quickly damp the inclinations of the two planets, requiring some later excitation to explain the nonzero inclination required by the TDVs," the authors write.

An illustration of a protoplanetary disk. It's possible that the planet was pulled into the inner system with other planets inside the protoplanetary disk. But disks tend to flatten orbital inclinations. So something else would've had to happen to explain the exoplanet inclinations. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle (SSC) - February, 2005

There are other possibilities, but they're outliers that "only operate in specific regions of the space of possible planetary orbital parameters," and only an accurate understanding of the system's overall architecture could confirm any of them. The researchers don't have that yet.

These are the types of solar system architectures that intrigue astronomers because they hint at new processes. Somehow, components of the system have interacted in ways that have produced a very unusual situation: a pair of massive planets close to their star. Not only that, but we can watch their interactions play out over only a few years, which is very rare.

"Our dynamical modeling reveals that the perturber is likely of Saturn-mass or greater and in a mean-motion resonance with TOI-2535b, making this an unusual system that contains two short-period giant planets," the authors write. "The TDVs measured for TOI-2535b represent one of the most extreme examples of planetâplanet interactions driving orbital evolution on human timescales."

If there were only a single close-in planet, a more ready explanation would offer itself. But because there's a pair, the researchers have to reach further for an explanation.

âBecause TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,â Yee said. âWe may be seeing a formation channel that doesnât happen very often but is very interesting.â

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.

#6479. Most Space Heaters Oscillate Side-to-Side. This Dreo Moves Air Upward for Better Coverage.

The powerful fan and rotating body poured out warmth in every direction.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s been a bit chilly as the cold weather has begun to set in. In that chilliness, I’ve broken out the cable-knit sweaters and undershirts, but I can’t very well type in gloves. In order to beat the freeze in the cavernously large bullpen with high ceilings and large windows that is our office, I needed a space heater built for the moment. That space heater is the Dreo Whole Room.

The Dreo Whole Room space heater oscillates both horizontally and vertically to cover larger areas of space and better distribute heat throughout a room. At the same time, the device is also extremely powerful, blasting heat at three different temperature levels and fan speeds. Particularly for drafty rooms or larger spaces, this is a space heater that not only got my attention but helped get my blood flowing.

I loved the Dreo both for quick, on-demand heat as well as for more sustained use over several hours throughout the day. Even in the drafty office, there was a notable difference in temperature almost immediately, and it spread well beyond just my desk when oscillating.

The most notable feature on the Dreo Whole Room Heater is the dual oscillation. With both horizontal and vertical oscillation, the space heater is capable of spreading heat in more directions and bringing the temperature of a space up more holistically. This design choice prevents cold spots in a room and provides a more overall warmth so you don’t have to be in direct line of the heater in order to feel its effects.

In my own use, the feeling is noticeable. When left on and oscillating for a few minutes in a side room in our office, I walked back into a noticeable shift in temperature. The room was nearly as warm in the far corners of the space as it was within a three-foot radius around the heater.

While the oscillation is great for heating up full rooms, there’s still a lot of additional customization available to tinker with. The space heater comes with three different heat levels as well as three fan speeds so you can choose the intensity and strength of the air. While this is great for short bursts of time, I preferred using the temperature setting.

This setting allowed me to choose a specific temperature, and the Dreo would automatically run, slowing down as it neared it, and occasionally turning back on to maintain it. If you expect to use the space heater for extended periods of time, this mode makes it easier to both not overheat and save a bit of energy. That said, the Eco mode is your best bet for cutting down on energy costs.

Once I know that the heating power is powerful enough to be worth the money, the next concern is always safety (despite it probably deserving to be first). On this front, the Dreo Whole Room Heater is a solid choice.

The space heater not only has tip-over protection and a safety plug but also automatically shuts off if overheated and has a three-second child lock to prevent them from accidentally switching settings inadvertently. My only real issue with the child lock is that the three-second time might not be enough time to prevent a kid from unlocking the features and making changes.

As far as a space heater goes, I really only want to make sure it heats well and is safe to use. On those fronts, the Dreo Whole Room Space Heater gets the job done.

However, the Dreo goes far beyond what’s expected. The dual oscillation helps warm up larger spaces with greater speed and efficiency, and the safety features make me feel comfortable leaving it on when I’m out of the room for periods of time.

If you have larger rooms you want to warm up without turning on your central heating, or simply want to get a fuller warmth as opposed to an incredibly localized one, the Dreo Whole Room is a good horse to back.

#6477. The Chandra X-Ray Observatory Unmasks a Supernova Impostor

When is an apparent supernova not really a supernova at all? That's a tough question to answer, especially since no supernovae have been observed in the Milky Way in the telescope era. The ones that astronomers see are mostly many millions of light years away in distant galaxies.

SN 1987A was the closest modern supernova, but it exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is still more than 160,000 light years away. And that was before the Hubble launched, and studying its aftermath was difficult. Now we have automated supernova surveys that scan the sky for exploding stars. One such survey detected what seemed to be a supernovae in 2016, in a distant galaxy.

Sometimes, a star exhibits variations in brightness before it explodes as supernovae, and that can create confusion around what's actually happening. That describes the object detected in 2016.

That object was a massive star in a distant galaxy that's showing behaviour associated with a typical supernova explosion. Supernovae explosions are the final act of massive stars that reach the end of their lives, and their prodigious energy output can light up the sky. That's what this star does, sort of.

But unlike a supernova with a single explosion, this star has a volatile outburst every 113 days, something that no supernova can repeat. In an effort to understand what's behind these repeated outbursts, astronomers turned to one of NASA's workhorse space telescopes, the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Chandra's exceptional angular resolution sets it apart from other x-ray observatories, and it can pick out faint sources in detail at great distances.

The volatile star, named AT 2016blu, has about 33 solar masses and is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, around 30 million light years away. AT stands for astronomical transient, and blu is a sequential suffix that tells us the star was the 1,685th transient reported in the year 2016. AT 2016blu is also called a luminous blue variable (LBV), and was first discovered in 2012 by an automated supernova search.

LBVs are rare, and as noted above, exhibit powerful variations in both their brightness and their spectra. Their variability is usually considered to be unpredictable, but in this case, it's periodic.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal has an explanation for AT 2016blu. It's titled "AT 2016blu: Accretion-powered Outbursts in a Luminous Blue Variable and Compact Object Binary," and the lead author is Mojgan Aghakhanloo, a Virginia Institute of Theoretical Astronomy Origins Fellow at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

"We present the first X-ray detection of the supernova (SN) impostor AT 2016blu in NGC 4559," the authors write.

Astronomers are calling AT 2016blu a 'supernova impostor' because LBVs are often detected in supernova searches. "Supernova (SN) impostors are transient events associated with massive stars that are often initially discovered in SN surveys," the authors explain. "However, because their outbursts are less energetic and less luminous than true SNe, and because the star is expected to survive, they are subsequently classified as SN impostors."

Unlike a supernove, AT 2016blu appears to have a nearby companion that triggers the outbursts.

"AT 2016blu exhibited 27 detected quasiperiodic (â¼113 day) outbursts between 2012 and 2026 June, presumably triggered by periastron passages in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is a â³33 Mâ luminous blue variable (LBV)," the authors explain.

Chandra had observed AT 2016blu by accident in 2001-2002, but that was before its first documented outburst. Those observations were actually aimed at another nearby ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX), NGC 4559 X7. XMM-Newton, an ESA x-ray observatory, also observed AT 2016blu four times while looking at NGC 4559 X7. So there's a collection of happenstance observations of the region.

âFor 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,â said lead author Aghakhanloo. âUntil we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldnât figure out what was making this happen.â

Overall, astronomers observed 27 outbursts of optical light from the supernova impostor between 2012 and 2026. That's one burst about every 113 days, something no supernova can do, since they're destroyed in their explosive outbursts.

âThis starâs behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly itâs not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,â said co-author NÃºria Torres-AlbÃ , also of the University of Virginia. âTo understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data that was timed so that weâd observe the star when it was in an outburst.â

Once it was known to exhibit outbursts, the researchers watched it in optical light leading up to its next predicted outburst. Then they used Chandra to observe it in x-rays, since it's the only x-ray telescope powerful enough to discern AT 2016blu from the other nearby x-ray source, ULX NGC 4559 X7, which is much brighter than the supernova impostor. "We monitored the sourceâs visual-wavelength variability around its predicted outburst time and triggered a Chandra Target of Opportunity (ToO) program in 2026 March, obtaining observations with detections over five closely spaced epochs," the authors write.

The left panel shows a stacked Chandra image of all five target-of-opportunity observations taken during the 2026 March optical outburst of AT 2016blu, in a span of 4 days. The right panel is an XMM-Newton image of the same sky region. XMM-Newton is not as powerful as Chandra, and cannot resolve the two sources. The image is dominated by ULX NGC 4559 X7, much brighter than AT 2016blu. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

âWe suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,â said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. âThe dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.â

Chandra's x-ray data from its 2026 outburst shows that AT 2016blu is 100 times brighter in x-rays than in its data from 2001 to 2002. This is best explained by a binary companion. "These outbursts are most likely triggered by periastron encounters in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is an LBV," the authors write. The secondary is almost certainly a neutron star or a black hole. As they orbit each other, the LBV ejects material that finds its way to the secondary. The material orbits the secondary at very high speeds in an accretion ring, and that heats it up until it emits x-rays.

Based on the x-ray luminosity, the researchers estimate that about 2.7% of Earth's mass is transferred during each outburst.

As is often the case, the researchers had to rule out a potential background source, and for that they relied on Chandra, too. "The alternative to a genuine counterpart to AT 2016blu would be a background quasar with a coincident position," the researchers explain. "This quasar, furthermore, would have brightened at a time coincident with our observations, and thus the AT 2016blu outburst."

These panels are all Chandra images. The first five are from Chandra's observations of AT 2016blu during the ToO campaign, and it's clearly visible during its outbursts. The sixth panel is a stacked image of the region outside of an outburst, clearly showing no background quasar. "No source is detected in the stacked archival images prior to the first observed optical outburst of AT 2016blu, when it was a stable system," the researchers explain. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

"AT 2016blu represents the first observationally known LBV system with a compact companion," the authors write. "Previously studied LBVs either lack X-ray detections or show luminosities consistent with windâwind collisions in massive-star binaries."

Its discovery could shed light on other, similar transient phenomena. Many stars show changes in brightness before they explode as supernovae, and maybe some of them are similar to AT 2016bu. "The discovery of an LBVâcompact-object binary undergoing accretion-powered outbursts also connects AT 2016blu to a growing class of models in which massive starâcompact object binaries explain a variety of pre-SN transient phenomena," the authors explain.

The next step, as is often the case in observations of new types of astrophysical objects, is to find more of them.

"Expanding the sample of such systems is therefore essential to better understand the evolutionary pathways and physical mechanisms connecting SN impostors, LBVs, and interacting SNe," the researchers conclude.
