#6441. The 5 Best Gas Snowblowers Can Move Mountains (of Snow)

Too much snow to shovel? A snowblower offers the most power and the longest runtime.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter will be here before you know it, which means the best time to prepare for cold weather and potential snowstorms is now. While snowfall isn't as regular in many parts of the country as it used to be, storm systems can still dump big piles of snow at once. When it comes time to dig out, there are few tools as effective as a gas-powered snowblower.

Although electric snowblowers are certainly attractive—they are relatively lightweight, easy to use, and require little maintenance—they lack the raw power and long runtime you’ll need if a storm drops 18 inches of snow or more on your home, especially if you have a large driveway.

The best gas snowblowers can carve a path as wide as two feet—giving you plenty of room to walk through as much as 21 inches of snow on a single pass. And if you keep a spare tank handy, you should have more than enough runtime to clear your walks and driveway multiple times. If you’re in the market for a heavy-duty snow removal machine, we’ve researched and tested plenty. These are our top picks, plus a breakdown of everything you need to know to pick out the best gas snowblower for your home.

If you have a large driveway and get a lot of snow, this is the machine you want. This big Ariens has a 30-inch-wide clearing path and an ideal clearing depth of 18 inches. Its four-stroke gas engine means no fussing with mixed fuel, and the push-button electric start means you don't have to exhaust yourself with a recoil starter.

This is a stout machine that is made for working. Test Editor Brad Ford runs a similar machine on his property, which is extra demanding because he has a gravel driveway. Thankfully, this machine can handle gravel surfaces thanks to its adjustable skid shoes, which allow extra clearance between the base of the auger and the driveway.

This machine is not for everybody; smaller properties will be well-served by the smaller picks below. But for those with the capacity for this kind of snowblower, this Ariens is a solid choice.

This model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899, which is a good price point considering many two-stage snowblowers are more than $1,000. But it’s not short on features. This model gives you push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight for clearing snow at night. After all, the snow doesn’t always stop falling during work hours.

It also handles fairly deep snowfall with a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height. To help keep the blades safe on uneven terrain, you can adjust the height to handle that, or clear areas like gravel paths. Another feature we really like is the ability to turn the wheels 180 degrees to help make tighter turns. Features like that can’t always be found at this price point, which is why it’s our pick for a snowblower that packs a lot of value.

A medium-sized property that only gets a moderate amount of guaranteed snowfall each year doesn’t need a two-stage snowblower. A single-stage model is fully capable of clearing your driveway and sidewalks. This model from Toro has plenty of power to get that job done, with a 212-cc engine that should cut through even wet snow and throw it up to 35 feet away. This model is also self-propelled to help you do the pushing.

Some of the features we like on it are a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute from the handle and a push-button electric start—both make operating it a little bit easier.

Like most single-stage snowblowers, its intake is lower than a two-stage, so you can only expect to clear snowfall up to 10 inches. If you commonly get much higher than that, you’ll want a more robust snowblower, but if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter, this Toro will get the job done.

The Toro SnowMaster 824 QXE stands apart from other single-stage gas snowblowers because of its intuitive controls and powerful engine. With a 252-cc engine, it chews rapidly through snow, carving a 24-inch path through banks up to 18 inches high.

With a lighter, more compact frame and automatic steering, the 824 QXE is easier to maneuver than its dual-stage counterparts. And, unlike most single-stage snowblowers, the auger is slightly elevated, so you can use it on gravel surfaces without having to worry about sucking rocks into it.

This machine also brings lots of special features to make the clearing process easier. Not only is it self-propelled, but it features a “personal pace system” that automatically adjusts the snowblower’s speed to match your walking pace, so you don’t have to fumble with speed controls. If you're familiar with Toro's self-propelled lawn mowers, this system should be familiar.

The snowblower also has a push-button starter and joystick-operated chute control, which makes it easy to adjust your snow output on the fly. If you’re looking for a snowblower to clear up to 18 inches of snow from a small to medium-sized driveway, the SnowMaster 824 QXE is a worthy choice.

This snowblower from Murray is another great example of a two-stage snowblower from a respected company that doesn’t cost more than $1,000. It doesn’t have some of the extra features like our best value pick—namely, a headlight and a 180-degree wheel rotation—but it otherwise matches it in size and power.

It also has all the primary features you would want, including an adjustable chute that lets you aim the snow where you want, push-button electric start, an auger that can propel snow up to 40 feet away, and a self-propel drive with six forward speeds and two reverse speeds.

Something unique to the model, however, is a set of 15-inch snow-terrain tires that handle icy and rocky conditions better than others. Wheels are something other brands can skimp on, but Murray hasn’t done that here. If you have gravel paths or older sidewalks that present a challenge, this model is likely up to the task.

Gas snowblowers are the best tools for heavy-duty snow removal jobs at home. They’re effective against snowbanks piled up to two feet high, and can clear out larger areas, including wide driveways and walking paths. If you live somewhere that gets hit by many large snowstorms each season, and you’ve got a considerable-sized area to clear, then this is what you need.

Not everyone needs a gas snowblower, though. For homes with smaller needs, they may feel like more trouble than they’re worth. Gas-powered machines require more maintenance. Plus, they’re usually quite heavy, which makes them hard to use on tiered walkways with steps. If heavy snow is a rare occurrence, we’d recommend going with an electric snowblower instead, which will be more nimble and won’t produce any fumes.

Most gas snowblowers feature either a single-stage or two-stage mechanism, depending on how the snowblower collects, processes, and expels snow.

Also known as “snow throwers,” they use an auger to pull in snow, break it up, and throw the snow out through the chute in a single action.

These also use an auger to pull in snow, but then mash it up with a spinning impeller before spitting it out through the chute. Separating the snow-pulling and snow-crushing/throwing mechanisms allows the two-stage snowblowers to move snow more quickly and throw it a longer distance, which can be helpful when clearing larger driveways. These robust machines also work better on gravel, since their augers are slightly elevated and won’t draw rocks into the tines.

With an extra component that requires a more powerful engine to operate properly, two-stage snowblowers are generally larger, making them more difficult to maneuver around tight spaces. If you have a small walkway or gardens with uneven ground to avoid, operating one may feel unwieldy. As you might expect, they also cost more than their single-stage counterparts.

As with deciding between electric and gas snowblowers, consider the size of the area you normally clear before picking a single- or two-stage model. Single-stage snowblowers work well for clearing walking paths and the average-sized two- to four-car paved driveway. Dual-stage models are ideal for clearing deep snow from long paved or gravel driveways.

A snowblower’s clearing width and intake height determine how much snow it can move with each pass. The larger the snowblower’s intake, the more quickly you can get the job done.

Most single-stage gas-powered snowblowers have intakes that range from 22 to 24 inches wide, while two-stage snowblowers can have intakes that are up to 32 inches wide. The height of the snowblower’s intake, which is sometimes referred to as “clearing depth,” indicates the maximum snow depth it can handle. The intake height for a gas snowblower ranges from 18 to 21 inches.

Purchasing the snowblower with the widest, tallest intake may seem like a no-brainer, but keep in mind that there’s a correlation between intake dimensions and the overall size of the snowblower. The largest gas snowblowers will have a harder time maneuvering through tight turns. Ultimately, you should choose the smallest option that can effectively clear the paths you need and the amount of snow you expect to see.

A snowblower's job is to take snow in front of you and move it somewhere out of the way. With a more powerful snowblower, you can send the snow farther away. That’s crucial when you’re clearing out a large space, and you need to pile it up dozens of feet from you. Single-stage gas snowblowers can launch snow up to 40 feet, while two-stage snowblowers have a snow-throwing range of 50 feet or more.

Some gas snowblowers come equipped with a throttle on the dashboard that allows you to adjust the throwing distance by changing the speed of the impeller, allowing you to target a specific snow-piling plot.

Beyond the basics, many gas snowblowers have additional features that make them easier to use. Since they weigh hundreds of pounds, many are self-propelled, so you don’t have to push them forward. Most also have electric starters that eliminate the need to pull a starter cord. Some even have built-in power steering that automatically slows one wheel for easy turning.

Other quality-of-life features abound: You may find dashboard controls that allow you to change the chute direction and snowblower speed with one hand, LED headlights for late-night (or early morning) jobs, and handlebars that heat up to keep your hands nice and toasty as you work.

We selected the best gas snowblowers based on recommendations from the Popular Mechanics test team, as well as research and personal testing experience. Some of our picks were recommended by Popular Mechanics test editor Brad Ford, who has logged hours and hours testing snowblowers over the years. The final lineup includes a mix of single-stage gas-powered models for small to moderate driveways that can house four to six cars, and larger two-stage models that can clear snow from the longer and larger driveways you usually find on rural properties.

There are a few things you need to do to make sure your gas snowblower runs smoothly through the season:

First, check the oil level between each use and top off as needed. You should change the oil once a year, even if you didn’t use your snowblower all winter.

Change the spark plug at the beginning of each season to ensure it starts smoothly. A dirty spark plug can make it difficult to get your snowblower going, especially in extreme cold.

Lastly, small gas engines require plenty of airflow to run smoothly, so check the air filter once a season and replace it if it's dirty.

Snowblowers use unleaded gasoline—the same thing you put in your car—which begins to degrade after about 60 days. Running a snowblower with old fuel can clog the carburetor and make the engine hard to start, so you should never store your snowblower with fuel left in the tank.

Before putting your snowblower to bed for the season, either run the fuel tank dry or add fuel stabilizer, which keeps gasoline fresh for up to 24 months, to the tank. If you use fuel stabilizer, run the snowblower for a minute or two after adding it to the tank to circulate it through the engine.

A snowblower should be able to handle the lion’s share of your snow removal duties, but you should definitely keep a snow shovel around to clean up whatever the snowblower leaves behind. You may also want to save the gas and dig out with a shovel after a light, soft snowfall.

#6440. Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain

Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.

Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.

In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in Science, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.

GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.

The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.

Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.

A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.

They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.

Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek9987

#6439. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752]

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

The lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also shows what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.)

Farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

The clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

A 2010 satellite photo shows the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

#6437. Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top

Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.

Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.

Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.

Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.

Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.

The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.

As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.

Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”

The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.

Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2026.1677796

#6436. LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON

According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

#6435. The 7 Best 3D Printers for New Makers, No Matter What You’re Making

Whether you’re printing parts, toys, tools, or making art, a 3D Printer is an incredible tool for crafting and creating.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s an example of why I love 3D printers. Over the holidays, the drain in my bathroom sink broke. Part of the pop-up assembly snapped, and the stopper was stuck in the down position. I didn’t have time to run to the hardware store, so I searched for an at-home solution. I checked online and found that someone had created a 3D-printable version of the exact part I needed. And 30 minutes later, part in hand, I repaired my sink.

3D printers can replicate virtually any part or product through a process called additive manufacturing, which assembles physical objects by layering a pliable filament or building material. Most consumer 3D printers work with various plastics, but there are printers that work with a wide range of materials including metals, ceramics, composites, wood, and more.

In the decade since 3D printers first exploded onto the consumer tech scene, these tools have become much easier to use. It used to be that you’d spend more time fiddling with the printer than using the product that you just printed. While they are still hobby-grade (read: expensive) tools, modern printers make it easy to set up a print, and you don’t have to babysit your project to make sure everything comes out okay.

Buying a 3D printer today isn’t too different from buying a table saw—you’ll need to do some research to find one that fits your space and can print what you want to print. Once you have it, you can focus on designing and printing everything from toys to tools to tech.

I’ve taken the time to test some of the most highly rated and popular 3D printers to highlight the best for new users. These are some of the easiest printers to use, and should allow technically minded newcomers to get up and printing as quickly as possible.

I’ve been a maker and tinkerer for decades, and have used 3D printers both professionally and as a hobby, printing everything from board game pieces to replacement parts for appliances. I’ve seen first-hand how diverse the 3D printing community is, and that we have a wide range of needs.

A tabletop gamer needs a different type of printer than a print farm operator, or an artist, or a maker. On top of that, there are a ton of nuances to consider when comparing 3D printers from size and speed to print quality and affordability. For this guide, I specifically prioritized printers that are easy to use. I imagine that, if you’ve come to Popular Mechanics for advice, rather than a deep message board or 3D printing influencer, there’s a good chance that you’re just starting out and haven’t put down roots in the community. That’s okay! Welcome! I’m here to help you get started.

Nearly all of these printers are new models, released in the last year. There’s one exception, the Creality Ender 3 V3 SE, which is our “Easiest to Use” pick. It was tested, though, by contributor Sascha Brodsky to see how well it holds up against newer models.

I tested each of the printers we recommend by printing all kinds of things, from detailed busts and decorative lithopanes to peg board organizers, table saw rails, and shop vacuum accessories. I sent a core group of models through all the printers, and pushed the boundaries of individual printers with a range of sizes, styles, and filament types. All told, I stacked up more than 100 hours of print time per printer.

I focused on printing with common filaments that a new user would most likely use, such as polylactide (PLA), polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). During testing I used the manufacturer’s slicer and – when possible – their branded filament as well. I printed models taken off the manufacturer’s online services, as well as third-party sites. I selected a variety of models, from functional to decorative, and from large to miniature. I tried to push all the printers in terms of consistency, performance, and precision.

I also recorded how long it took to set up each printer, from opening the box to producing a completed 3DBenchy benchmark model. (Or “box to Benchy” time, as I like to call it.) I also had more subjective measurements, such as how intuitive the printer interface and slicer are. I made note of anything I found confusing in their UI, and I tracked whether they needed babysitting to complete a print. I also tracked any failed prints, to see if the printer had an error detection system, or if it continued to run through the failed print.

And through it all, I identified which printers made the process easiest, from set up to printing and troubleshooting. Once I got them through all that, I was able to see which ones stood out from the rest in terms of price, performance, and features.

Released in the U.S. last November, the Bambu P2S is Bambu’s mid-line printer, falling between the entry-level A1 and their premium H-Series models. This is hands-down the most user-friendly 3D printer I’ve ever operated. From setup and basic operations to remote printing, it’s so easy to use it almost feels like running on autopilot.

In the last few years, Bambu has revolutionized the 3D printer industry by bringing more intuitive, beginner-friendly features to the market. Their business is based on creating a full ecosystem for users to explore. Bambu provides their own filament with RFID chips on the spools, so the printer can change its settings to match that specific filament’s needs. And their Maker World website is full of models and tools, including one-click projects (such as RC cars), that start a 3D print and simultaneously ship out any hardware or electronics needed to complete it.

Bambu encourages—some critics would argue “pressures”—users to use all of these integrated services. The situation is not unlike the “walled garden” of Apple’s iOS App Store, which curates a library of beautifully designed products that are accessible and easy to use, at the expense of some creative freedom for both users and developers.

Regardless of how you feel about this kind of manufacturer ecosystem, though, the P2S is an impressive machine. It’s an intuitive system that’s easy to use, and works right out of the box. Of all the printers I tested, the Bambu P2S was the only one that never gave me a single connection issue, and any failed prints were identified and paused to allow me to address the issue.

That ease of use even extends to the Bambu mobile app. Most 3D printers have a mobile app that allows you to track progress or view your print progress in real time through a camera, but Bambu’s Handy app is on another level: It connects directly Bambu’s Maker World, allowing you to set up prints remotely from your phone, automatically handling slicing. To be honest, I didn’t think I’d use the app, but I quickly found myself breaking out my phone while watching TV and sending a quick print to the P2S. It was so easy to use, it just became second nature.

For new users, I loved Bambu’s tutorial library, including tutorials in both text and video. This is even true for the “experimental” services in their Creator’s Maker Lab, where users can create their own models using a range of manual and AI tools. I tried a few of these with moderate success. (It struggled with photos of people wearing glasses, and it tended to generate disturbing results, including a 3D model that combined two of my dogs into a single nightmare creature that would be at home in a Cronenberg film.)

No printer is perfect, of course. The P2S uses a single nozzle to print multiple colors, which means the machine needs to reset, purging the old color and cutting some filament for the change, before resuming the print. Doing that once isn't a big deal, but complex prints may have hundreds or even thousands of color changes.

This takes its toll on both efficiency and print time: In a couple of complicated prints, I found that the printer discards three to four times as much filament as it used for the actual print. Likewise, I printed a single-color mask piece in 2 hours and 4 minutes, but a 3-color version of the design took an astronomical 19 hours and 30 minutes.

One other minor issue: it struggled with any filament that wasn’t well-wound. I buy a fair amount of this stuff, and some manufacturers ship filament that’s loosely wound. I can get away with using it on a single-color printer or even a multi-toolhead machine. But with filament changing designs like the P2S, the filament gets bound up. I never had this issue with Bambu filament, or with well-wound 3rd party filament.

The Bambu P2S exemplifies how 3D printers have improved over the past few years. While other printers may have a specific task where they perform better, but the P2S is so incredibly easy to use, which makes it a great all-around option for beginners who may or may not know what they plan to print most. It’s the closest thing to a “set it and forget it” experience that you can get with a 3D printer.

The Centauri Carbon is fast, affordable, and fun to use. It’s also a rare find for entry-level printers looking to enter the hobby with a low investment, with print quality and features that are typically seen in more expensive models. It doesn’t have many of the bells and whistles that I love from my other picks, but it delivers great value for its price, and it’s a perfect starting point for general use printing.

It has a strong sense of fun in its design. For example, the included waste-bin model that clips to the back of the printer isn’t just a bland box, it’s a tiny model of the Centauri Carbon. I felt the slightly playful nature of the design reflected a desire to make things enjoyable for the user, something that included keeping setup simple, with a box to Benchy time of one hour, 11 minutes, the fastest time I’ve found to date.

Elegoo seems to want to balance a streamlined UI with robust options. Their custom version of the Orca slicer tucks away some features in the name of streamlining, but they’re still there if you go digging. (That may be a good thing or bad thing, depending on how much you like to tinker with settings.) A recent software update added an integration for Nexprint, Elegoo’s 3D model site, which makes it much easier to download projects straight into the slicer.

One simple UI choice that I appreciated is that the mobile app has a clear pause button, so if something looks wrong, you can stop the print before it completely goes off the rails. It’s a weird bit of psychology, but just being able to clearly see it made me more comfortable during long print jobs.

The Centauri Carbon was noisier during operation than the other printers I tested, but silent at rest. (It has relatively hard feet, which seemed to cause more vibration in the bench than other printers.) That left me more inclined to leave it on, which opened the door for me to queue up projects more spontaneously.

One issue worth noting: When the Centauri Carbon debuted, Elegoo announced that it would have a multi-color option sometime in 2025. Now, finally, a multifilament printing option is slated for Fall 2026 availability with the $55 Canvas upgrade.

Out now is the full-blown second iteration of the Centauri, the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo (which comes with the Canvas upgrade) and will run you $450, while the original Carbon costs about $415—$360 for the printer, plus $55 for the Canvas upgrade.

Read the Full Review of the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 3D Printer Here

The QIDI Q2 can print with more durable materials that can withstand abuse from high heat and prolonged sun exposure. It lacks some of the added conveniences found on Bambu’s P2S or Snapmaker’s U1, but it’s priced accordingly. That makes it a standout if you’re looking for a fully enclosed, single-color printer that can print more robust materials.

There are two specific areas where the Q2 excels: First, it’s a great choice if you want to print materials that require a higher nozzle temperature and/or could produce a higher volume of fumes. Second, it keeps most of the customization options readily apparent, making it a good printer if you know you like to tinker with settings and dial-in custom quality and performance.

The Q2 was easy to unpack and to set up, with a box to Benchy time of 1 hour and 20 minutes. (The unit I tested did not include the QIDI Box multi-color kit, which meant I only had to set up a single filament feed.) That said, setup may pose a couple challenges for first-timers: The quick-start guide was light on details, and occasionally skipped steps. For example, there’s no mention of the cover in the setup instructions. It’s not a dealbreaker—chances are that you’ll realize you can put the cover on top—but I found myself wondering more than once if I’d accidentally missed something. Once the Q2 takes over the process and begins to calibrate, though, setup is a breeze.

I found almost everything about the Q2 worked right out of the gate. If you find that you need to make tweaks, though, there is a library of helpful tuning tutorials with photos. (I wish someone handed me these back when I started 3D printing).

It has single-band, 2.4 Ghz WiFi, which allows you to send files directly to the printer, and an interior camera so you can monitor prints remotely. The Q2 is relatively smooth and quiet while printing, though it keeps a fan running even when idle, ironically making it both among the quietest and loudest printers I tested.

It has an AI error detection that can potentially spot the “spaghetti” strands of filament caused by a failed print. Mine went off twice, alerting me in time so I could make adjustments before the print went off the rails.

I did run into an issue with a clogged nozzle after about 60 hours of printing. When I took off the cover, I pressed on the nozzle fan and found it had snapped its support struts. I’m not sure if the fan went bad and caused the clog, or if I damaged the fan when I pressed on it. Regardless, QIDI sent a replacement fan and hot end, and I was up and running with relative ease.

While my tests focused on basic filaments such as PLA, PETG, and TPU, the QIDI Q2 has a higher-temperature nozzle (370 degrees Celsius) and an interior box temperature of up to 65 degrees Celsius. This allows it to print with more robust materials, like polycarbonate (PC) and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS). It also ships with a hardened steel nozzle, allowing it to print materials like carbon fiber (CF) or glow-in-the-dark filaments, which would damage softer brass nozzles. If your long-term printing goals include using your printer to make automotive parts, or other, more durable items that need to withstand high temperatures and forces, I think the Q2 can help you learn the ropes, and get where you want to go once you know what you’re doing.

I have a lot of affection for the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE. My colleague Sascha Brodsky recommended it as our “easiest to use” pick when it launched in 2023, and for good reason. It was one of the first 3D printers to come mostly assembled, with clear instructions and enough user support to get you up and running, as well as features like automatic bed leveling that made the printer far easier to use than other models available at the time.

Today, the V3 SE is older than most of my recommendations, but it’s still an attractive (and very affordable) option. In its heyday, it was an outstanding selection for those new to 3D printing, and helped bring features like auto-leveling and partial assembly to market at an affordable price. Three years later, it still compares favorably with newer models in terms of setup time, with about an hour and a half from box to Benchy, putting it only a little behind the single-color enclosed printers on our list.

It's worth noting that even a few years in, I use this printer fairly regularly, especially when printing TPU or other flexible filaments. Softer plastics are generally susceptible to print issues, especially in enclosed printers that tend to run hot. If you’re not careful, you can end up with a sticky, stringy mess of a print, or even a clogged nozzle. Luckily, the Ender-3 V3 SE’s open frame and durability manages heat well, and gets the job done with ease. I’ve never had a problem, and that's what keeps me coming back.

That said, the design has started to show its age. It doesn’t have WiFi, so you’ll either have to set up a controller (such as a Raspberry Pi) or shuttle an SD card back and forth. With a max toolhead speed of 250 millimeters per second, it’s far slower than modern printers like the QIDI Q2 which can run at up to 600 mm/s. It also has a smaller print bed, no camera for remote monitoring, and no error detection.

The Ender-3 V3 SE is capable of producing attractive prints, but the quality you’ll get is dependent on your ability to dial in the settings. It doesn’t automate settings or provide a seamless integration with online models. It also doesn’t have advanced calibration features like input shaping, which updates the printer’s settings to account for environmental vibration. Instead, you’ll need to hand-calibrate all those settings. On the plus side, it’s wide open to tweaking and adjustments, making it a great choice if you like to tinker and optimize performance.

The Ender-3 V3 SE is a venerable printer, and still has a lot to offer. Its user-friendly design was ahead of its time and, while it’s no longer our pick for Easiest to Use, the V3 SE remains a great choice for users who want to use flexible filament or are working with a tighter budget. It’s often available on sale, bringing its cost below $200, and if you’re willing to be patient, Creality sells factory-refurbished models for even less.

The Snapmaker U1 set crowdfunding records when it launched on Kickstarter, thanks to its clever multi-head system that keeps four nozzles preheated and loaded with filament. It can change tool heads on the fly, rather than changing filament fed through a single nozzle. With no need to purge older filament, the U1’s design cuts print time and dramatically reduces waste. Seeing this printer go head-to-head with a filament changer, the choice is clear: I'll take the Snapmaker every time.

The U1’s setup kit is top-notch. It has an extensive, step-by-step assembly document, with full color images of each step, and a QR code that links to a video walkthrough. I loved that it shipped with extra parts, so a broken part doesn’t bring you to a complete standstill until you order a replacement.

Assembly and calibration took longer than other printers, because with four print heads, there’s essentially four times the work. It had a box to Benchy time of 2 hours and 49 minutes, more than double single-color printers like the QIDI 2 or Elegoo Centauri Carbon. (For an apples-to-apples comparison, I printed an actual Benchy model; the full-color test model that comes with the U1 adds a few hours of time, though the result is an adorable baby dragon, which immediately scored me points when I gifted it to my wife.) Even with the longer setup time, it never felt onerous.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that the U1 comes with a generous amount of starter filament. It ships with four colors, each with 500 grams of filament, compared to most printers which ship with only a few grams, just enough to print a test Benchy. Snapmaker filament rolls also have RFID, so that you don’t need to manually enter the filament details.

Unfortunately, it does not ship with a lid for the enclosure, or any kind of filter in the case. This can become a problem when you print with materials that require higher nozzle temperatures. Snapmaker doessell a lid, along with a HEPA/activated carbon air filter, for $150. With the lid attached, the internal chamber can reach up to 50 °C, allowing the U1 to print higher-temperature materials like ABS and PC. Obviously, though, it’s annoying to pay extra for a feature that you might see as a core component of the printer. (If you’re open to a DIY solution, though, the U1 forums have a discussion thread where users are sharing their own custom tops. This is why I love the 3D printing community!)

Overall, printing was a breeze, whether using Snapmaker or third-party filament. The U1’s AI error detection worked well, pausing prints if any debris was detected, and allowing me to fix it or cancel the job without wasting more filament. In fact, I had no problems with the U1's hardware at any point during testing. Where I did run into headaches was with the software. As it stands, Snapmaker's version of Orca is sluggish to load, and I had to reconnect the slicer to the printer every time I opened the software. The software is still in beta, and I expect this will be improved before release. Hardware this polished deserves a quality app to go with it.

Testing the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra was an exercise in both delight and frustration. There’s no disputing its print quality, especially when I produced beautifully detailed game miniatures. But I ran into regular obstacles on the path to those beautiful prints, in the form of poor or even confusing documentation. In a review focusing on ease of use, those pain points really stood out.

Resin printers like the Mars 5 Ultra are especially popular with gamers, who print miniatures for tabletop games. These small figures tend to be packed with details, and printers like the Mars 5 Ultra can generate layers as thin as 0.01 mm, 10 to 20 times thinner than a typical FDM printer. If you want sharp visual details, resin printing is the way to go. The Mars 5 Ultra is an especially good way to learn about printing with resin, thanks to a pair of features that make it more user-friendly than its peers.

First and foremost, it has a tilt-release resin vat that reduces the suction forces between the build plate and the vat. When the build plate bed lifts up after each layer is complete, the vat tilts, creating an angle that makes it easier to separate. (Think of it like pulling off a sticker or a bandage -- it takes far less force if you start on one corner.) Since the tilt-release makes separation easier, your settings don't have to be dialed in quite so precisely in order to get a clean separation from the vat, and support points can be slightly smaller. As a result, you spend less time adjusting settings or removing support marks, and more time enjoying your finished prints.

It also has a very helpful error detection feature, which is great for new printers. If the Mars 5 Ultra detects foreign objects in the vat—usually chunks of supports or models that have fallen off the print plate—it will pause operation and send a notification. That can minimize damage to the model you’re printing, and prevents debris from getting trapped, which could also crack the vat itself. (In general, I think any feature that keeps toxic resin where it belongs is a big value-add.) Both the vat and error detection save time and reduce the frustration of a failed print. They’re also more commonly found on printers that cost twice as much as the Mars 5 Ultra.

Unfortunately, the standout design is somewhat undercut by Elegoo’s confusing and contradictory support documentation. The instructions told me to install Chitubox (an industry-standard slicer) from the included USB stick. But the only slicer on the USB was Elegoo’s SatelLite slicer. Now, I actually like SatelLite, but it’s not what they told me to expect. What’s especially frustrating is that Elegoo actually has a fantastic unboxing video with a clear, easy to follow walkthrough. But there’s no mention of it in the manual and no QR code linking to it on the packaging. So I only saw it when I stumbled across it online.

Setup aside, this is an excellent printer. It’s well designed and easy to use, and produces quality prints with minimal fuss. (Or at least minimal fuss for resin.) The touchscreen is easy to read and well laid out, with an easy to understand user interface. It is a little small, but it’s sensitive enough that I didn’t need to tap twice, even while wearing gloves.

I also love Elegoo’s optional in-box heater. I picked one up when the temperatures plummeted. Since I’d set up the printer in my garage, I thought I’d fall behind on testing. But the heater installed easily and worked spectacularly well. Before I knew it, I was churning out prints even though the weather was well below freezing. But that heater was the reason I was able to get a full test run on the printer, even during a polar vortex.

The Bambu X2D costs about $100 more than the P2S, and for that additional cost it delivers active heating, better venting, and a dual-nozzle design, letting you print more demanding materials faster and with less waste.

Most enclosed printers depend on passive heating, maintaining the internal temperature simply with the captured heat from the nozzle and print bed. By contrast, the X2D has a built-in heater allowing the internal chamber to reach temperatures up to 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius). The X2D’s active heating also allows this temperature to be consistent, making it much easier to reliably print materials like Nylon and ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene).

If you want to print material that can withstand the heat of an engine bay or exposure to the elements, the X2D is a fantastic choice. In addition to the active heating, it has an external carbon and HEPA filter to reduce fumes and airborne particles. It also has a dual-nozzle design that reduces waste when printing two-color models, and allows for easy support printing and removal.

The downside to the X2D is that I found it’s surprisingly prone to minor issues and inconveniences. I ran into a weird error when printing the Benchy model that shipped on the internal memory, and had to do additional tweaking to align models and the prime tower on the print bed. None of these would be unusual from another manufacturer, but Bambu has made a name for themselves by delivering the smoothest possible user experience. The X2D doesn’t quite live up to that standard.

It’s a very good printer for both standard and high-temperature filaments. And for the relatively small step up in price, it compares favorably to the P2S if you want to move beyond decorative items and start creating durable objects that can withstand a real-world environment.

There are two types of 3D printer built with home users in mind: FDM and resin. (While other types of 3D printers are available, they’re intended for industrial use, with a learning curve and price tag to match.) As a rule of thumb, FDM printers are faster and produce more rugged prints than resin, while resin printers excel at fine detail.

Fused deposition modeling printers (FDM) are like a hot glue gun for plastic. They feed a strand of plastic filament through a heated metal nozzle, laying out the print onto a heated metal bed. They’re cleaner and easier to use than resin, and require less safety precautions. They tend to have larger print volumes, but they don’t produce prints that are as highly detailed as resin.

Resin printers, on the other hand, create layers of material by dipping a flat bed into a vat of liquid resin, then curing a layer of material with UV light. (It’s similar to the process of making candles, where you dip a wick into wax repeatedly.) They are typically more complicated to use, as the models have to be washed and cured after printing is complete. Printer resins are toxic until cured, and using resin printers requires significant safety precautions. Resin printers produce highly detailed prints, prized by users ranging from tabletop gamers making miniatures to the dental offices, creating surgical implants and guides.

Both types of printing have their pros and cons, depending on your space, your style, and what items you want to print. Generally speaking, FMD printers are good for larger items, items that need to be more durable, or when you need to turn around prints quickly. They are also a good choice if you’ll be printing in areas with less ventilation or if you’ll have children or pets around while printing. Resin printers are a better choice if you want outstanding detail, and have room to set up a cleaning station for your prints.

FDM printers are usually described by the head movement (either CoreXY or bed-slinger) and whether or not it’s enclosed or open frame. CoreXY printers move the head left to right, and front to back. On a bed-slinger, the head moves left to right, but front to back adjustments are made by moving (“slinging”) the bed itself.

Enclosed printers are just that–enclosed on all sides. These are typically CoreXY printers, and allow for higher temperatures and provide filtered vents for filaments that produce more fumes. They also usually cost more than open-bed printers.

To start printing, you’ll need some 3D models and software (called a slicer) to send them to your printer. Luckily, some of the best options are free.

Every 3D Printer uses some type of slicer software, which allows your printer to analyze objects and create a blueprint for making a 3D printed copy. True to its name, it creates a digital model and “slices” it into anywhere from one to a few thousand printable layers, creating the building blocks of a 3D print design. The result is a detailed set of instructions for printing, called G-code. When you load a design, your printer follows the G-code to assemble the design, layer by pre-sliced layer.

Printer manufacturers provide a proprietary slicer or an open-source slicer customized for their specific machines. For testing purposes, I used the slicer provided by the manufacturer. Honestly, once you get used to one slicer, they’ll all feel pretty similar.

Creating your own print designs isn’t necessary, though, if you don’t feel compelled. There’s no shortage of sites with free or paid 3D print designs that you can download and print. Once you have a little bit of experience printing, there’s a whole world of printable tools and products to explore within the 3D printing community.

When a plastic part breaks, there’s a good chance someone else has run into the same issue and created a 3D version of that part to download and print. Many printer manufacturers support some kind of community site, where users can upload, remix, and review 3D models.

Yes, when used properly. Both FDM and resin printers pose safety risks during operation. FDM printer risks include the hot end of an FDM nozzle and fumes from melted plastic. Resin printers pose more risks, as resin itself is toxic, and should not be allowed to touch unprotected skin, and should only be used in an area where the fumes can be safely vented outdoors. Resin printers also use UV light to cure the prints, which can damage your eyes if not properly filtered.

FDM safety precautions are fairly straightforward. First, don’t stick your hand in the print area while the printer is running. This may sound obvious, but it’s surprisingly tempting to do, since sooner or later you’ll spot a bit of loose filament or some other bit of debris laying on the bed in the middle of a print. It’s very easy to reach in and grab that debris without pausing the print -- but the print head moves very fast and without warning. That nozzle is probably around 300 degrees celsius / 580 Fahrenheit, and having it slam into your knuckle can leave a puncture and a burn.

Second, make sure the room where you operate the printer is well ventilated. Proper ventilation is especially important when using high VOC filaments. These include acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and acrylonitrile styrene acrylate (ASA), but the fumes will vary by manufacturer, so err on the side of caution.

Resin requires more extensive safety precautions. You’ll need to invest in PPE such as nitrile gloves, a respirator (use filters rated for VOCs and not just dust debris), and possibly UV safety glasses. When resin printing, venting is even more important. In most cases it’s easy to safely vent your 3D printer, but if you’re concerned, consider getting an air quality monitor to ensure that you’re working in a safe environment.

Your primary expense using a 3D printer is your printing material, which will be plastic filament for these printers, but could be other materials with more advanced models. You can buy a one-kilogram reel of PLA filament for about $12 to $19. If you need a specialty filament, you’ll likely pay double that amount, and prices can go much higher for premium materials.

Then there’s the hit to your electric bill. FDM printers typically use about 50 to 100 watts to operate, depending on what material you’re printing and the ambient temperature. If your electricity is 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, your printers will likely cost less than 2 cents per hour to operate.

Lastly, there will be other costs over time: You may need replacement bed plates for FDM printers, or post-processing supplies for resin printers. Other parts may break and need replacing, as well.

Once you have a print and some compatible printing material, all you need to do is figure out what and how to print. I recommend new printer users pick up some calipers ($30 or so, but you can get away with a $10 set). You can actually 3D print most of the other tools you’ll use. In fact, printing storage bins and organizers for your printing tools is a great way to learn the ropes while making useful prints.

#6434. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

This research received support from the National Institutes of Health (DP2AI177967, S10OD023402, S10OD032141, R35 CA263850, S10 OD032265), Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation, Gateway Foundation for Cancer Research (G-22-800), Cancer Research Institute Lloyd J. Old STAR Award (CRI3447), Sy Holzer Endowed Immunotherapy Fund, The Pittsburgh Foundation (MR2023-134140), National Institute of Allergy & Infectious Diseases (R01AI171483, R01AI166598), National Cancer Institute (P30CA047904, R01CA277473, P50CA121973, P50CA097190), and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center Skin Cancer and Head and Neck Cancer SPOREs.

A very interesting study. Nothing in medicine is adverse-effect-free!! However, if this study only involves changing the gut environment and a high-fibre diet, which everyone should be on anyway, why not just tell people on cancer immunotherapy to abide by the regimen? I also understand that the effect needs to be tested in animals, but the poor mice have to have cancer and then be treated with the new hypothesis.
