#6384. Scientists Warn of a Disturbing Rise in Vitamin K Deficiency Among American Newborns

Only about one in five infants diagnosed with vitamin K-related bleeding had received the shot, U.S. health records show.

Babies are born with little vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable to bleeding that can cause permanent brain damage or death. A single shot helps protect against that danger. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended one dose injected into a muscle for newborns since 1961, and a growing number of American parents are choosing to skip it.

That trend has coincided with a sharp rise in diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). A nationwide study found that their rates increased by 216% and 347%, respectively, between 2017 and 2025, while the percentage of newborns receiving injectable vitamin K fell from 97.7% to 95.0%. The findings were published on November 5, 2026, in JAMA Pediatrics.

Vitamin K activates specialized proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Newborns receive too little through the placenta, absorb it poorly through their digestive systems, and get little from breast milk. The injection addresses a deficiency at a time when its consequences can be severe.

Classical VKD occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and causes bruising and bleeding from the umbilicus, or belly button. Late VKD, which occurs between 1 week and 6 months of age, carries a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage, or bleeding inside the skull. That bleeding can lead to seizures, permanent brain damage, or death.

Refusal of the shot has increased over the past decade. Previous studies found that the proportion of newborns who did not receive intramuscular vitamin K rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024.

To investigate the consequences of that trend, Elizabeth Wolf, M.D., MPH, led the new nationwide study. Wolf is a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU and an associate professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine.

The researchers analyzed de-identified electronic health records from a large national database covering health systems across the United States. Their analysis included more than 11 million infants aged 0 to 6 months who were born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later and received care between 2017 and 2025.

Only 40% of infants diagnosed with VKD and about 19% of those diagnosed with VKDB had received vitamin K shots. About 7% of infants with VKD and 2% of those with VKDB also had a diagnosis of intracranial or intracerebral hemorrhage, meaning bleeding inside the skull or within the brain tissue itself.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf said. “We found that the answer is undeniably yes, with the rates of VKD and VKDB multiplying over the course of our study.”

The researchers caution that the simultaneous decline in injections and increase in diagnoses does not prove causation. Wolf considers other explanations unlikely, however, because behaviors and diseases that increase the risk of VKD remained constant or decreased during the study period.

The study’s co-authors included Steven Woolf, M.D., director emeritus of the VCU Center on Society and Health and a professor in VCU School of Medicine’s Department of Family Medicine, Evan French, MS, of VCU’s C. Kenneth and Dianne Wright Center for Clinical and Translational Research, and Darya Shokouhi Niaki, Pharm.D., of the VCU School of Public Health’s Department of Biostatistics.

Wolf connected the findings to growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals.

“Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals. We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”

Like childhood vaccines, the researchers say, vitamin K has been “a victim of its own success,” with many parents unaware that refusing the shot can have serious lifelong consequences. Wolf says more research is needed to determine how best to communicate the seriousness of vitamin K deficiency and encourage use of the medication in newborns.

“We should continue to follow these trends moving forward since the rates of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding may continue to rise if vitamin K refusal keeps increasing. We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication,” Wolf said.

Reference: “Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants” by Elizabeth R. Wolf, Evan French, Darya Shokouhi Niaki and Steven H. Woolf, 5 November 2026, JAMA Pediatrics. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.5794

#6382. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6381. Ancient Tomb Reveals That People Were Getting High on Cannabis 2,800 Years Ago

The oldest directly dated evidence of intoxicating cannabis use comes from a Scythian tomb, suggesting the plant’s mind-altering effects had a place in ancient burial rituals.

About 1,000 cannabis seeds recovered from a princely tomb in southern Siberia could not, on their own, tell archaeologists whether anyone had used the plant to get high. Cannabis, one of today’s most commonly used psychoactive plants, has also supplied oil, fiber, and medicine, and its flowers, leaves, and resins rarely survive to help distinguish among prehistoric uses.

The tomb, in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva, belonged to high-ranking members of Scythian society, a horse-riding culture of the Eurasian steppe. Researchers investigating the burial found another source of evidence in preserved human hair from its central chamber.

Dr. Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern’s Institute of Archaeological Sciences and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, led the international research team and is the lead author of the study, published in Science. “The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,” he says.

By directly radiocarbon dating six seeds and combining those measurements with other dating results, the researchers determined that the seeds were placed in the grave in the early eighth century B.C. The findings provide what is currently the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of cannabis use for its intoxicating properties. “The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,” says Caspari.

In an earlier publication, the team described the remains of 18 horses that had once been arranged on the burial mound. Several dozen additional horse sacrifices and scattered human bones have since come to light. “In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well,” says Caspari.

To investigate whether cannabis compounds had entered the bodies of people buried there, the researchers analyzed the hair using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other methods. Mass spectrometry helps distinguish compounds by the mass and electrical charge of their molecules or fragments. Several hair samples produced clear signals consistent with cannabinol, or CBN, a compound that can form through the oxidation of tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the main intoxicating compound in cannabis. The team also detected weak signals whose masses were consistent with THC.

“This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body,” says Caspari.

The researchers interpret the hair results as evidence of cannabis use, although the analyses cannot reliably establish how much was consumed or determine with certainty how its active compounds entered the body, such as through inhalation or ingestion. Later archaeological sites in Central Asia have yielded chemical residues of cannabinoids, compounds found in cannabis, in vessels and on heated stones that clearly indicate inhalation. The Tyva hair samples do not establish a particular method of consumption.

The recovered seeds likely came from wild plants, and the findings do not reveal how much THC those plants contained. It also remains unclear whether people specifically cultivated cannabis for its psychoactive properties or selected or cultivated plants for higher levels of active compounds.

The team is continuing its investigation. “We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,” says Caspari. “DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.”

Reference: “Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago” by Gino Caspari, Timur Sadykov, Daria Fomicheva, Jegor Blochin, Dominic Armbruster, Oliver Happel, Natalia Ryabogina, Kseniia Boxleitner and Robert Spengler, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aeg3800

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6378. Stonehenge’s Mysterious Six-Ton Stone Has Scientists Searching Across Britain

Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone has led scientists from Wales to Scotland, yet even its most detailed geological examination has failed to reveal where it came from.

Scientists have spent more than a century trying to determine where Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone came from. Once thought to originate in Wales, the massive sandstone slab has since been traced geologically to northeast Scotland, but its exact source remains unknown. Now, the most comprehensive geological investigation yet has ruled out several proposed locations and provided new clues to guide the search.

Published in the Journal of the Geological Society, the study examined the stone’s mineral composition, chemistry, and other geological characteristics. Measuring 4.9 meters (16 feet) long and weighing about six metric tons (6.6 US tons), the Altar Stone could offer important insights into how prehistoric people transported massive stones across Britain thousands of years ago.

The latest investigation brought together observations of the Altar Stone itself and detailed examinations of fragments held in museum collections. By comparing its structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic characteristics, the team assembled a set of identifying features that potential sources must match.

No location examined so far in northeast Scotland’s Orcadian Basin has met all those criteria. That leaves the stone’s birthplace unresolved but gives future fieldwork a clearer target. Study leader Duncan Pirrie, emeritus professor at the University of South Wales, said:

“This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone’s composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.”

The findings build on earlier work that redirected the search away from Wales. Richard Bevins, honorary professor in Aberystwyth University’s Department of Geography and Earth Sciences, said:

“For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge’s most enduring mysteries.”

Nick Pearce, emeritus professor of geochemistry in the same department at Aberystwyth University, emphasized the value of eliminating candidates: “In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.”

Stonehenge took shape through several construction phases between around 3000 and 1600 BC. Moving its stones across great distances was part of that achievement: the smaller bluestones traveled approximately 225 kilometers (140 miles) from west Wales.

Establishing where the Altar Stone began would give researchers a crucial geographical anchor for investigating how it reached the monument. The researchers hope that fingerprint will ultimately lead them to the source and shed new light on the effort behind one of prehistory’s most remarkable engineering achievements.

Reference: “Searching for the origin of the Stonehenge Altar Stone: new sedimentological, petrographical, mineralogical, geochemical and isotopic constraints” by Duncan Pirrie, Richard E. Bevins, Rob A. Ixer, Nick J. G. Pearce, Peter Turner, Matthew R. Power, Stephen Hillier, Andrew C. Morton, Ian Saunders, Sergio Andò, Marta Barbarano, Andrew Horbury and Gregory D. Price, 5 November 2026, Journal of the Geological Society. DOI: 10.1144/jgs2026-090

#6377. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

With the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

But everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

One downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt, 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no issues at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#6375. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6374. CT Scans Reveal the Secret of a Mysterious 400-Year-Old Lock

X-ray scans cracked an Elizabethan padlock’s code, revealing how a centuries-old security mechanism worked without damaging an unusually well-preserved piece of maritime history.

For more than 400 years, a brass combination lock recovered from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast kept its secret. Lost when a violent storm wrecked the Ann Francis, the remarkably well-preserved Elizabethan lock still had working letter dials, but no one knew the four-letter combination needed to open it.

Opening it more than 400 years later meant working out its four-letter code without damaging an exceptionally well-preserved Elizabethan artifact, a challenge that brought museum specialists together with researchers more accustomed to studying bones.

The lock came from the Ann Francis, which was returning from Spain when a ferocious storm blew it off course on the evening of December 28, 1583. The ship wrecked on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot, leaving its extraordinary cargo buried beneath the sand for centuries.

Dredging and storms eventually stripped away layers of sand, exposing traces of the sixteenth-century hoard. Metal detectorist Peter Hughes discovered most of it over 21 years, between 1996 and 2017. The finds, recovered by Hughes and other metal detectorists, were subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales).

“When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition. When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked,” said Hughes, finder of the hoard.

What the lock once protected remains uncertain. Researchers believe it secured a small chest containing valuable items, and its position near a collection of Spanish silver coins and two coin weights recovered from the wreck offers some clues. It may have guarded those objects or a chest holding valuables that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.

To investigate the mechanism, museum experts worked with specialists at Cardiff University using micro-CT, a form of X-ray imaging that can reveal fine details inside an object. Dr. David Williams, a postdoctoral research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility in the university’s School of Engineering, explained the advantage of examining the lock this way.

“Micro-CT scanning allowed us to look inside the lock without damaging it.”

The task was to connect the letters visible on the outside with the concealed parts that determined whether the lock would open. Williams could examine those relationships in the scan, then pass the combination to the museum team for the physical test.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination. We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us. I had to wait until later that evening for the museum team to test the combination, so getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” said Williams.

The four letters were ANCE, and when the museum team tested the combination, the centuries-old lock opened.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!” Williams said.

Its remarkable condition and connection to a shipwreck with a known date make the lock especially valuable as a historical find. Deciphering the combination also leaves a more personal question about whoever chose those letters.

“Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve. Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” said Alastair Willis, senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru.

The lock is currently on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea alongside other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard. They include rare gold coins dating from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain and a boatswain’s whistle recovered from the wreck.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6370. A 6-Million-Year-Old Whale Had a Face So Strange Scientists Thought It Was Crushed

A newly identified prehistoric whale had unusual adaptations that may have allowed it to hunt along the seafloor millions of years ago.

An ancient whale that lived millions of years ago had a skull so dramatically distorted that its face appeared pushed to one side. Its bony nostrils were displaced entirely to the left, and its oversized snout curved sharply downward. Scientists have identified the animal as Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale with the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a cetacean.

The fossil dates to the Late Miocene, approximately 6.3 to 5.6 million years ago, and belonged to a whale measuring about 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) long. Researchers believe its skull may also represent the greatest facial asymmetry known in any mammal.

Most vertebrates have skulls that are approximately symmetrical, with corresponding structures on either side of the head. Toothed whales are an exception. Their skulls have evolved asymmetrical shapes to accommodate specialized organs involved in producing sound and echolocation, allowing them to navigate and detect prey underwater.

“Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked,” explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study. He investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich and is now an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale’s unusual anatomy suggests a feeding strategy very different from that of modern sperm whales, which pursue squid in deep ocean waters. Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have been adapted for searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal seas. Its thick, tubular snout contained dense bone and hardened cartilage that added weight toward the front of its body. The snout angled downward by 31 degrees, while reconstructions of the joint between the skull and first neck vertebra suggest the animal could lower its head by as much as 55 degrees.

“The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, study co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.”

Unlike some modern marine mammals that forage along the bottom, Scaphokogia lacked specialized facial whiskers and visual adaptations associated with locating prey in sediment. Researchers therefore suspect it relied on its unusually developed biosonar system to detect food hidden in soft seabed deposits. This remains a hypothesis based on its anatomy rather than direct evidence of its hunting behavior. Its specialized ecological niche apparently disappeared as ocean conditions changed near the end of the Miocene.

The skull was recovered in the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru, a desert region famous for exceptionally preserved marine fossils. Benites-Palomino encountered the specimen in 2015 while working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its extreme shape initially raised the possibility that geological forces had distorted the skull after the animal died.

“The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy – that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years,” says Benites-Palomino. “But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The researchers chose a species name that reflects the animal’s unconventional appearance. Huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and describes something extravagant, flashy, bizarre, or aesthetically excessive.

“In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant, or difficult to categorize aesthetically,” says Benites-Palomino.

“When we looked at the proportions of this whale – with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout – it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.”

Reference: “Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales” by Aldo Benites-Palomino, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Florencia Paolucci, Jorge Vélez-Juarbe, Alberto Collareta, Apolline Alfsen, Alton Dooley, Dan Omura, Mario Urbina, Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, 9 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11074-2

#6369. Scientists Discover Mysterious New Fish in the Red Sea – and Have Never Seen It Again

Scientists discovered a tiny new fish species in the Red Sea but have never found it again, suggesting it may live mostly on deeper reefs that remain largely unexplored.

In Greek mythology, Charon ferried the dead across a river into the underworld. People were traditionally buried with a coin to pay for the crossing. That tradition helped inspire the name of a newly described fish species from the northern Red Sea, Charon’s pygmygoby (Trimma charon).

“One of the most striking features of the new species is the golden spots scattered across its tail fin,” said study leader Viktor Nunes Peinemann of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins.”

The tiny fish is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters long, roughly half an inch and two-thirds of an inch.

The new species resembles the pallid pygmygoby (Trimma anaima), a fish found from East Africa to the Pacific but never recorded in the Red Sea. Genetic data suggest the two are close relatives, although further work is needed to confirm that relationship.

“While one species seems to have spread across much of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, its closest relative appears to have stayed in the Red Sea and evolved separately for millions of years,” said Peinemann.

Researchers collected the two specimens in May 2023 at Walih Island, at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. They were found 30 meters, about 98 feet, below the surface, the maximum depth of the team’s scientific diving. Extensive searches of similar habitats since then have produced no further sightings. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” said Peinemann.

The team suspects that the encounter took place at the shallow edge of the species’ range. The fish may be more common on largely unexplored mesophotic reefs below 30 meters, where sunlight is faint. That possible habitat provides another connection to its mythological namesake.

“These dark, deeper, unexplored reefs could be viewed as a kind of ‘underworld’ beneath the shallow, well-lit, and better studied reefs most of us are more familiar with,” he said.

“Red Sea reefs below that depth almost certainly hold more undiscovered gobies.”

The discovery brings the number of known Trimma species in the Red Sea to 11, making it the region’s most species-rich goby genus. At least nine appear to live nowhere else in the world. To help researchers distinguish them, the paper provides an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, along with photographs and field notes describing where each lives.

The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys. Peinemann is based in the Marine Science Program within KAUST’s Division of Biological and Environmental Science and Engineering. His co-authors are Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen of KAUST, and Sergey V. Bogorodsky of the Senckenberg Research Institute and Natural History Museum Frankfurt, Germany.

“Knowing which species are present, how to accurately identify them, and where they live, is the most foundational step to building a stronger understanding of these species and ecosystems,” said Peinemann. “They still have many secrets and deserve much more attention.”

Reference: “Trimma charon, a new species of pygmygoby (Teleostei, Gobiidae) from the Red Sea with a key to the Red Sea species of the genus” by Viktor N. Peinemann, Sergey V. Bogorodsky, Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen, 24 September 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1293.204097
